Later capitals on the same ground, Seleucia, Ctesiphon, and Baghdad among them, prove the pull of the spot. Chapter two turns to the city site itself and the digs made there in recent years.
57003-the-intimate-letters-of-hester-pio:
Oswald G Knapp edited The Intimate Letters of Hester Piozzi and Penelope Pennington, covering 1788 to 1821. John Lane published the volume at London and New York in 1914, with thirty illustrations. A portrait of Mrs Piozzi, engraved from a drawing, fronts the book. The first chapter sets the two women in place. It treats Mrs Piozzi and the blue-stockings, and Penelope Weston's family, the Salusburys.

Piozzi married Thrale in 1763, was widowed, and married the musician Piozzi in 1784. Foreign travel and a return to England in 1788 end the groundwork. The Piozzis in Hanover Square, a Scotch tour, and a Welsh visit follow. Harriet Lee's romance and Mrs Siddons enter the story. The September massacres and the French Revolution darken the letters. Miss Weston marries William Pennington in 1792.
57055-baily-s-magazine-of-sports-and-pas:
The eighty-fifth volume of Baily's Magazine of Sports and Pastimes binds the six monthly numbers from January to June 1906, published by Vinton at London. Baily's was the sporting man's magazine: hunting, shooting, fishing, racing, and cricket, with portraits of the riders and masters of foxhounds of the day. George Hirst, the cricketer, fronts the volume, and the Earl of Huntingdon opens the biographies.

The contents run from the breeds of British salmon and the education of the puppy to distemper in hounds, dressing flies, borzoi dogs, and cricket topics. A piece on the development of the modern motor shows the times changing under the horse world. For the Edwardian sportsman this was a half-year's companion, part record and part club talk.
57361-the-21st-missouri-regiment-infantr:
N D Starr and T W Holman compiled Historical Memoranda of the Twenty First Missouri Regiment Infantry Veteran Volunteers, printed at Fort Madison, Iowa, in July 1899. A front account traces the book to a veterans group formed in 1888. Holman called the first meeting at Arbela, Missouri, on his own charge that year.

Survivors had scattered across Missouri and more states after the war. No bid to keep the unit alive came till that call. Large crowds came and yearly meetings have been held since. In 1896 Holman and Starr were made regimental historians. Their draft was read at Edina in 1898. Holman then revised it for print for the association. The book keeps names, marches, and battles of the unit from 1861 to 1866.
57459-reprint-of-two-tracts-1-an-essay-o:
Two Medical Tracts is a reprint of two works by J. P. Marat, doctor of medicine. The first is An Essay on Gleets, and the second An Enquiry into the Nature, Cause, and Cure of a Singular Disease of the Eyes. The reprint was edited by James Blake Bailey, librarian of the Royal College of Surgeons of England. It came out in London in 1891 from Percival and Company, for private circulation only.

The edition ran to 84 copies, of which 75 were for sale. The essay on gleets states its aim in its own subtitle. It points out the flaws in the method then in use for such complaints of the urethra. It then marks out a sound way of curing them. The tracts show the famed leader of the French Revolution in his first trade, as a doctor of the age.
57869-the-orlando-innamorato:
William Stewart Rose turned a famed Italian chivalric poem into English in a mixed form, part prose and part verse. The Orlando Innamorato tells of Orlando in love, and it stands as the needful lead in to the greater Orlando Furioso. Rose kept sample stanzas in the same verse form as the source, set within his prose tale.

The Italian source came through the reworked form made by Francesco Berni from the work of Boiardo. In his long preface Rose tells how Lord Holland urged the task on him as a mate to his Furioso work. Knights, the fay Morgana, gardens, and wild quests fill the old tale. Rose aims to keep its grave tone true.
57962-select-specimens-of-natural-histor:
Select Specimens of Natural History is the fifth volume of a Nile travel work. The travels sought the source of the Nile through Egypt and Arabia. Abyssinia and Nubia complete the route of that famous search eastward. Ruthven printed it at Edinburgh in the year 1790 for Robinson. A Greek tag from Aristotle fronts it: Africa always bears something new.

A verse from First Kings praises Solomon speaking of trees and beasts. Contents open with an introduction, then plants, shrubs, and trees in order. Papyrus, balessan balm, sassa, and myrrh fill the early plant heads. Ergett, ensete, and kol quall follow among Abyssinian growths described there. Beasts, fowl, creeping things, and fishes complete the natural history.
58256-the-russian-army-and-the-japanese-:
General Kuropatkin's The Russian Army and the Japanese War, volume one of two, was published by Dutton in New York in 1909, printed in Great Britain. Captain Lindsay translated it; Major Swinton edited it, having written The Defence of Duffer's Drift. The subtitle states the brief: historical and critical comments on Russia's military policy and power, and on the campaign in the Far East.

The translator's preface opens with a Times judgment of February 1904. The General stood higher than any other Russian officer, at home and among soldiers the world over. If any man could turn Russia's bad position in the war, Kuropatkin was thought the man to do it. Maps and plates accompany the volumes, and this first volume takes the policy and the opening of the campaign.
58770-beryl-of-the-biplane-being-the-rom:
Beryl of the Biplane, being the romance of an air-woman of to-day, is a war novel by William Le Queux, published by Pearson of London in 1917. Le Queux was billed on his list as the master of mystery. The contents open with The Mysterious Number Seven, then Mr Mark Marx and The Shabby Stranger. The Thursday Rendezvous, Concerns the Hidden Hand, and The Price of Victory follow.

The first chapter is set among night flyers at Brooklands. Beryl is asked whether she is flying the Hornet tonight; she was up three hours the night before, Zeppelin-hunting. Two raiders came in over Essex but were scared off by the anti-aircraft guns. A passage preserved in the copy widens to the men of that world. Passers-by in Pall Mall that June afternoon no doubt wondered why Ronald Pryor was not in khaki.
58786-the-queen-s-reign-and-its-commemor:
The Queen's Reign and Its Commemoration, a literary and pictorial review of the period, by Walter Besant, was published by the Werner Company in 1897, the jubilee year. The subtitle calls the book the story of the Victorian transformation, spanning 1837 to 1897. Seven chapters and a closing section on the commemoration fill it.

Besant opens with Sydney Smith, who late in life wondered how the young men of his time kept a decent cheerfulness amid change. Smith died in 1845, at the start of deeper changes he never suspected. Besant holds that the eighteenth century lingered in its ways until Victoria's reign began. One who lived through the reign, he writes, has been an eyewitness to a revolution. It transformed the country in manners and customs, in thought and in standards. Yet it happened silently, while each man minded his own small interests.
59480-the-malthusian-handbook-designed-t:
The Malthusian Handbook urges married people to limit their families within their means. Reynolds of New Cross, London, sold the sixpenny book to all readers. This copy is the fourth edition, dated to the year 1898. Its introduction opens on the problem of poverty in civilised states. Want has at times threatened the very base of society itself, it warns.

Revolutions sprang from folk who needed food and could not get it. Honest, industrious men are driven to despair for work and bread. Beneath the glittering surface lies a seething mass of want, it says. Destitution breeds crime and worse, with a long chain of harms. Overcrowding and squalor breed disease that travels to rich homes too. Society stands likened to a palace reared in a festering swamp. The handbook's answer is smaller families fitted to a man's wages.
59784-index-of-the-project-gutenberg-wor:
Index of the Project Gutenberg Works of Marcus Aurelius Antoninus is a reference volume compiled by David Widger. It gathers the contents of the emperor's works as issued by Project Gutenberg. Two titles are covered: the Meditations and the Thoughts of Marcus Aurelius. For the Meditations it prints tables of contents of the volumes and the book-by-book layout of the whole.

The Meditations falls into twelve books, with an introduction, appendix, notes, and glossary. The index then lists paragraphs by their first lines. The first book opens with what Marcus learned from his grandfather Verus: to be gentle and meek. Entries follow for his upbringing, for Diognetus, Rusticus, Apollonius, Sextus, and Fronto, each keyed to its opening words. Later samples in the copy include maxims on doing one's earnest duty as a Roman and a man.
60242-the-purchase-of-the-north-pole-a-s:
Purchase of the North Pole is a novel by Jules Verne, a sequel to From the Earth to the Moon. Verne is billed as author of Twenty Thousand Leagues under the Sea. The London and Edinburgh edition carries many pictures. Contents run to chapters on a north polar practical association first. To syndicate or not to syndicate follows.

The north pole is knocked down to the highest bidder in the third chapter. Old acquaintances and a polar coal field follow. Barbicane makes a speech, and public opinion changes in the middle heads. Works at Kilimanjaro and a waiting African tribe fill the late list. A front picture asks what the first inhabitant would say. A quoted talk in the text weighs whether a woman can become a great mathematician.
60595-half-around-pluto:
Manly Wade Wellman tells a science fiction tale first printed in Worlds of If in December 1958. Pluto is a coffin world, airless and utterly cold, and a wrecked scout rocket has left three men ten thousand miles from base camp, with ten days to get there.

While their officer, Lieutenant Wofforth, lies hurt with a broken arm and collarbone, Jenks and Corbett bolt together a sled from girders and bulkhead metal and fit it with a salvaged engine. Then comes the blow: the rescue ships have already left for Earth. The men must cross half of Pluto on their own. Readers get a lean story of grit at the edge of the sun's light.
60975-the-russian-army-and-the-japanese-:
The Russian Army and the Japanese War, by General Kuropatkin, gives the Russian commander's own account and judgment of the war with Japan. This second volume of two appeared in English in 1909, translated by Captain AB Lindsay and edited by Major ED Swinton.

The volume takes up the reasons for Russia's defeats. Kuropatkin blames weak training for battle, flaws in the army's structure and its men, and a lack of fighting spirit and drive in carrying attacks through. He describes how the army's system broke down under the strain of active service. Later chapters propose fixes: better senior ranks, stronger regulars and reserves, more fighting men in the infantry, and changes for the machine guns, engineers, guns, and horse. Maps and pictures support the text.
61044-the-anatomist-dissected-or-the-man:
The Anatomist Dissected, printed at Westminster in 1727 and here in its third edition, is a satire on the rabbit affair that had seized London. It is written in the person of Lemuel Gulliver, surgeon and anatomist to the kings of Lilliput and Blefuscu. Its target is the surgeon St André, whose narrative had lent credit to the pretended rabbit-bearer, and who confessed he had been imposed upon.

Gulliver affects to break his retirement only because his own travels are being neglected while the town thinks of nothing else. He grants the man's candor in confessing the cheat, and denies that candor excuses him: no surgeon with real skill in anatomy, he argues, could have been taken in. The price was sixpence, and the booksellers of London and Westminster sold it. The pamphlet belongs to the pack of tracts that hunted the imposture down.
61253-journeys-to-the-planet-mars-or-our:
Journeys to the Planet Mars, or Our Mission to Ento, is a book by Sara Weiss, published in New York in nineteen hundred three. Weiss had already written a romance of Mars, as the title page notes. Ento is her name for Mars, and Entoans are its people. Chapters open with an interview with a being called the Evon Thia.

Later chapters describe Mars and its special features, its lands, and its sensitives, the people who can make contact across worlds. Giordano Bruno appears as a chapter subject, linking old thought to the new mission. The book mixes travel tale, spirit teaching, and a claim of real journeys. It belongs to early occult writing about other planets.
61483-definitions-in-political-economy-p:
Definitions in Political Economy is a treatise by Thomas Robert Malthus. John Murray published it in London in 1827. Malthus held a chair of history and political economy at the East India College. An inquiry into the rules for defining terms comes first. Remarks on other writers follow.

The preface names the problem plainly. Economists quarrel because they use the same words in different senses. Malthus tests the usage of the French economists. He then examines Adam Smith chapter by chapter. Say, Ricardo, and Mill get the same treatment. A later chapter gives his own definitions. A summary argues for his measure of value.
61694-expedition-to-pluto:
Fletcher Pratt and Laurence Manning fly far in Expedition to Pluto, from the Winter 1939 issue of Planet Stories. The head blurb crowds the ship Goddard with peril. Captain McCausland, hero of the space fleets, nurses a secret plan for an Earth reborn. A scientist coddles treacherous test tubes, and a mate grapples an unseen horror that menaces a billion lives.

The tale opens as a broadcast from the ship. Now passing Phobos, the second moon of Mars, the voice reports. From here to the orbit of Jupiter lies the planetoid belt, the most dangerous portion of the voyage. The ship's armor may keep meteorites out, he grants, but one little world striking her ends the broadcast. The captain does not look well this morning, the voice adds.
62232-a-letter-to-a-country-clergyman-oc:
A Letter to a Country Clergyman, by a writer who signs as a sub-urban clergyman, was printed in London in 1805 for Hatchard, bookseller to Her Majesty. The pamphlet answers a country parson's address to Lord Teignmouth, president of the British and Foreign Bible Society. A Latin motto from Tertullian heads the title page.

The writer jokes that a kind friend put the address in his hands and that it shook his nerves as much as the lord's circular shook the parson's. He confesses he had joined the same Bible effort himself, lending his name and spare money before the address warned him of a plot. Irony carries a real defense of Bible societies against early church fears.
62476-conspiracy-on-callisto:
James MacCreigh spins a tale of revolt on Callisto in a story from Planet Stories for winter 1943. Peter Duane holds a secret that could make the rising win or fail, the opening warns. Yet his memory is gone, and he cannot tell which side he serves.

Aboard ship Duane faces Stevens, a tall white-haired free lance who supplied their cargo. Stevens offers Duane ten thousand dollars and tells him to let the matter go. Duane answers that he was promised fifty thousand and will have to kill the man. Their boss Andrias waits on Callisto, where they land that night. Readers get a hard pulp tale of pay, loyalty, and a man fighting blind in a plot he helped to build.
63040-a-minor-war-history-compiled-from-:
Martin Haynes printed A Minor War History at Lakeport, New Hampshire, in 1916, in an edition of sixty copies meant chiefly for his family. The book copies the letters he wrote home from the Civil War between 1861 and 1864.

Haynes served in Company I of the Second New Hampshire Volunteer Infantry. His letters went to Cornelia Lane, the girl he left behind him and later his wife of more than fifty years. His preamble says the letters hold no grand strategy; they record camp small talk, comrades, and the small facts of army life that official records leave out. He jokes that readers may move Grant and Sherman up a notch and leave him third.
63393-mind-stealers-of-pluto:
Mind Stealers of Pluto, a science fiction story by Joseph Farrell, ran in Planet Stories in the winter of 1944. Ron Barnard is a reporter who has stuck his nose into one story too many. The head note traces his trail: a lovely girl, a wily Chinese, and a drug ring that circles the whole system of planets.

The tale opens in Quong Kee's bar on Mars, the worst dive on the planet. Barnard hunts the dope ring that haunts the outer worlds. Two addicts at a corner table hear his very thoughts, since the drug neoin grants strange powers of sense. One of them charges him, teeth bared and hands like claws. A rogue spaceship and a rocket's red stream await at the story's end.
64060-advance-australasia-a-day-to-day-r:
Frank Bullen's Advance Australasia, in its second edition from Hodder and Stoughton in 1907, is a day-to-day record of a recent visit to Australia and New Zealand. It opens with a chapter called Then and Now, looking back thirty-four years to his first arrival. That first visit was made in a Boston-built sailing ship, in what he calls the palmy days of the Australasian liners.

Bullen went as a sailor in his youth and returned as a well-known writer on the sea. The contrast drives the book: ports, ships, work, and town life are all measured against what he remembers. He writes warmly of the young countries and their growth. Readers at home in Britain were his market, and the record keeps the plain, direct manner of his sea books.
64097-the-female-physician-containing-al:
The Female Physician is a heal book by John Maubray, a doctor of the craft, out at London in seventeen twenty-four. Its full name vows to hold all the ills that fall on that sex, in maids, wives, and widows. Their roots, signs, grades of risk, and ways to bar and cure all stand in its scope. Past that comes the whole art of the birth craft in its new form.

That art gives the marks a birth wife must hold and plain rules for the lay of wives in hard and strange births. The food and rule of life of both the mother and the child close that scope. In a long gift note Maubray scorns the flat ways of book gifts. A sound work stands on its own base, he says, and needs no great name at its front.
64266-escape-from-pluto:
William Oberfield's Escape From Pluto ran in Planet Stories in the fall of 1947. Marcius Kemble stands on the frozen face of Pluto and curses Earth into his plastic helmet. In the year twenty-two hundred, the planets are free states, and Kemble was made an example for trying to rule them all.

He had seized Mars by stirring up old grudges, then reached for the moon-system of Saturn. The Planetary Combine broke his forces, and an Earth ship dropped him by parachute on cold, far Pluto. The blurb warns that even the Plutonians underrate the glory to which they send him. Exile, in this tale, is where the plot begins, not where it ends.
64632-cargo-to-callisto:
Cargo to Callisto is a science fiction story by Jay Drexel, from Planet Stories of November 1950. A deck line tells of four Aarnian criminals fled into the Martian night in silence. The Patrol dragnet is airtight, but nothing human is what an Aarnian is, it warns. The tale opens on Mars, at the Great Canal, with swimmers at play.

Sarah rises from the canal sleek and brown as a seal, laughing at Joe. Joe Caradac ducks his wife again while Kent shouts from the bank unheard. A senior intendant grin hints at office rank inside the canal side horseplay. Pulp Mars, patrol duty, and alien fugitives drive this 1950 magazine tale.
6466-the-intellectual-development-of-the:
John George Bourinot traces the intellectual development of the Canadian people in a historical review prepared as one of a series on the Dominion's social, political, and industrial progress. Canadian history divides into three periods, he argues: under the French regime, from the Conquest to the Union of 1840, and from 1840 to 1867, with a new period since Confederation. Intellectual lethargy marked New France, while United Empire Loyalists shaped the provinces' political and social life.

Parliamentary institutions, improved internal intercourse, growth of education, and political progress widened thought, and the professional and educated classes grew rapidly. A mid passage notes universities rising even in small provinces: Manitoba's university, Prince of Wales College after the 1860 Charlottetown visit, and Laval in Quebec, first suggested by Bishop Bourget of Montreal. Bourinot writes Canada's mind coming of age.
64866-narrative-of-an-expedition-through:
Narrative of an Expedition through the Upper Mississippi to Itasca Lake is Henry R Schoolcraft's account of the 1832 expedition that fixed the true source of the Mississippi. Harper and Brothers of New York published it in 1834, with a sketch of the sources drawn from Lieutenant Allen's observations. The volume embraces an exploratory trip through the St Croix and Burntwood rivers as well.

The War Department sent the party into the Chippewa country to put an end to the hostilities between the Chippewas and Sioux. Schoolcraft dedicated the narrative to General Hugh Brady of the United States Army. What began as a peace mission ended as a discovery: Itasca Lake, the actual source of the great river, reached and named by this journey. Schoolcraft's narrative remains the primary record of the expedition, from the man who directed it.
65667-the-wolf-queen-or-the-giant-hermit:
The Wolf Queen, or The Giant Hermit of the Scioto, is a frontier tale by Captain Charles Howard. Howard was the author of The Elk King, a pocket novel from the same house. The tale came out in New York from Beadle and Adams, with a copyright date of 1872. Its contents list a fast run of chapters, from The River Combat to The Hermit and His Cave.

Jim Girty and His Prisoner stands third, then The Events of That Night and The Mysterious Death-Shots. Out of the Cave to Doom, Alaska in Her Frenzy, and Jim Girty Triumphs carry the action on. One of Alaska's Whims, The Fate of Well-Laid Plans, and The Moles on the Shoulder stand later in the list. The tale is a dime novel of the Ohio frontier, full of captives, caves, and fights.
6652-the-humorous-poetry-of-the-english-:
James Parton gathers the best short humorous poems in English, from Chaucer to Saxe, with notes on each poet. Narratives, satires, enigmas, burlesques, parodies, epigrams, and epitaphs all appear, drawn from the Anti-Jacobin, Rejected Addresses, Ingoldsby Legends, Blackwood's, Bentley's, and Punch. More than two hundred epigrams alone fill the pages.

Wolcott, Cowper, Lamb, Thackeray, Swift, Scott, Holmes, Burns, Byron, Hood, and many more lend their wit. Parton leaves out poems too local or too tied to their day to travel well. The Humorous Poetry of the English Language is a thick, merry anthology, made for dipping into again and again.
67198-constantino-brumidi-michelangelo-o:
Constantino Brumidi: Michelangelo of the United States Capitol is a biography by Myrtle Cheney Murdock, printed at Washington in 1950. Murdock dedicates the book to her son David, killed in action at Palermo in August 1943. A Senate speech of February 1880 stands at the front, praising Brumidi's love for the Capitol.

The contents open with Brumidi as an Italian refugee. Then comes his art in the Capitol, with colour reproductions of his frescoes. Later chapters treat the artist's pay, his American wife and children, and his works outside the Capitol. Pictures show the President's Room, singing cherubs, and a portrait of Columbus. Murdock restores the Capitol's painter to view.
67859-american-horological-journal-vol-i:
Volume one, number one of the American Horological Journal appeared at New York in July 1869. Contents promise watch and clock craft from the first page onward. Astronomy in its relations to horology leads, then watch and chronometer jewelling and hints on clocks. New tools, Greenwich Observatory, pinions, and a three pin escapement follow in order.

Shorter notes add English views of American watch making, letters, an eclipse, and diamond cutting. An equation of time table closes the number for working readers. The lead essay argues that star transits give the only true test of a timepiece. Mean sidereal time anchors every rate a maker can claim. A trade learns its science in its own new journal here.
68422-address-of-the-president-at-the-un:
Address of the President at the unveiling of the monument to General Sheridan is a printed speech of 25 November 1908. The Government Printing Office at Washington issued the address in 1908. It marks the unveiling of a statue to General Sheridan at the national capital. 

The address holds that the illustrious men of the nation should be commemorated at its capital. Sheridan, it says, will always stand high on the list of American worthies. He was not only a great general but a man of genius, with a touch of originality in his gifts. That brilliance, the speech warns, has in one sense hurt his reputation with the public. Men think of him only as the dashing cavalry leader of the war. In truth, the speaker insists, he was also a great commander of armies in full.
69439-physiological-economy-in-nutrition:
Russell Chittenden wrote Physiological Economy in Nutrition, issued by Stokes of New York in 1904. Chittenden directed the Sheffield Scientific School at Yale. He also taught physiological chemistry there. The study asks how little proteid a healthy man truly needs.

The experiments rest on many helpers and backers. Grants came from the Bache Fund and the Carnegie Institution. Horace Fletcher and a Dayton donor gave large gifts. The War Department kept a detachment of army hospital volunteers at New Haven. Photographs show the subjects at work in the gymnasium. Soldiers and named men pose front, back, and side for the record. The book measures food needs by close experiment rather than custom.
70359-the-history-of-the-damnable-life-a:
The History of the Damnable Life and Deserved Death of Doctor John Faustus, printed in 1592, appears here in a modernized edition by William Rose, lecturer at King's College, London. Routledge in London and Dutton in New York issued the book, with twenty-four pictures drawn largely from old woodcuts. The Second Report of Faustus, of 1594, on the deeds of Wagner, is bound in as well.

Rose's introduction treats the historical Faustus, the German Faust book, Faust in England, the German Faust drama, and the Wagner book. The chapbook itself opens with Faustus's parentage and birth. Then comes his turn to the devilish art: conjuring the spirit, the parleys with Mephostophiles, and the pact written in blood set in a saucer on warm ashes. The text is the source Marlowe drew on.
71814-the-railhead-at-kysyl-khoto:
The Railhead at Kysyl Khoto, by Allen Lang, was produced from Infinity for November 1957. A quoted message heads the tale, naming a Siberian railhead, a rocket pioneer, and the Moon. Its meaning made White Sands look trivial.

It turned a rocket engineer into a salesman, the blurb adds. The narrator opens in Washington summer heat. He has been told that during the simoom season in Morocco, Arab judges let confessed murderers off with a fine. The weather justifies homicide. Washington judges should be as lenient in summer, he thought. His cigarettes had gone limp with sweat, and tasted like burning damp wool. Readers get a hard boiled rocket tale of 1957.
71933-anthology-of-russian-literature-fr:
Leo Wiener, assistant professor of Slavic languages at Harvard, made this anthology of Russian literature in English dress, published by Putnam in 1902. This first part runs from the tenth century to the close of the eighteenth. A sketch of Russian literature opens the volume, treating the oldest period, the folklore, and the eighteenth century, and the texts follow. There is the treaty with the Greeks of 911 and the Russian Code.

Nestor's Chronicle tells the baptism of Vladimir and of all Russia, and the Kiev Chronicle and the Word of Igor's Armament carry the tale of Prince Igor's raid. Later pieces give the Domostroy, the great book of household rule, and the letters that Ivan the Terrible and Prince Kurbski exchanged in anger. Songs collected in 1619 and 1620 close the early record.
73071-in-korea-with-marquis-ito:
George Ladd, a Yale philosopher, wrote this account of Korea, published by Scribner in New York in 1908. Part one narrates his personal experiences traveling with Marquis Ito in Korea. Part two is a critical and historical inquiry into Japan's rule there, as his title separates the two.

The invitation opens part one, with first glimpses of Korea and life in Seoul following. A visit to Pyeng-Yang and Chemulpo fill the travel chapters in the contents. Part two turns to the problem in history, the compact between Japan and Korea and the protectorate, by a guest who praised his host and asked hard questions.
7449-memoirs-of-general-lafayette-with-a:
Marie-Joseph-Paul-Yves-Roch-Gilbert du Motier, Marquis de Lafayette, was the French hero of two revolutions. This volume joins his memoirs to the story of his last great visit to America. He arrived on August 15, 1824, and traveled through a nation eager to receive him. The tour ended at the celebration at Yorktown on October 19, 1824, the anniversary of the victory he had helped win.

The account records his reception by the people of the United States town by town, a farewell tour that became a national festival. Old soldiers, crowds, and officials all turned out for the general of their youth. The book preserves both Lafayette's own memories and the voice of a young republic honoring the man who had crossed an ocean to fight for its freedom.
7525-the-history-of-roman-literature-fro:
Charles Thomas Cruttwell, who inscribed this work to his former teacher, the Archdeacon of Middlesex, wrote his history of Roman literature for students and for general readers together. It runs from the earliest period to the death of Marcus Aurelius, covering the whole arc from rough early Latin to the polished literature of the empire. University and public school students were its first audience.

Cruttwell also hoped to reach those preparing for the Indian Civil Service and other advanced examinations, and any reader interested in the grand literature of Rome without being a professed scholar. The book moves author by author, genre by genre, through republic and empire. It remains a clear, old-fashioned survey, useful for anyone who wants the shape of Latin literature whole.
7787-a-complete-grammar-of-esperanto:
Ivy Kellerman's A Complete Grammar of Esperanto, with full vocabularies, teaches Zamenhof's planned language in plain, systematic form. A transcriber's note explains its 28 letters. English letters minus q, w, x, and y remain, plus six marked letters, with hats on c, g, h, j, and s, and a breve on u.

Where marks fail, Zamenhof's h-method or the clearer x-method can stand in, though the first blurs some sounds. The grammar that follows sets out sounds, word building, and use. It gives English speakers a full road into a language meant to cross borders without favoring any one nation.
7864-the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipaya:
Kisari Mohan Ganguli's translation of the Mahabharata of Krishna-Dwaipayana Vyasa, made from Sanskrit prose between 1883 and 1896, aims to hold a mirror to its author. The translator's preface vows to keep the author's imagery and language, even at the cost of smooth English idiom and taste.

It is easy, Ganguli warns, to dish up Hindu ideas to suit English palates; harder to let them stand in their own form. This volume, scanned at sacred-texts.com, offers the great epic of the Bharata war, duty, and fate in full, faithful prose for readers new to India's central story.
7883-expositions-of-holy-scripture-secon:
Alexander MacLaren's Expositions of Holy Scripture, in this volume, moves from Second Kings chapter eight through Chronicles, Ezra, Nehemiah, Esther, Job, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes. Early sermons treat Hazael, impure zeal, Jehoiada and Joash, methodical giving, and the spirit of power.

Later expositions give a kingdom's epitaph, divided worship, Hezekiah as a pattern of devout life, the rediscovered law, and the end of Judah. David's choristers, drill and enthusiasm, and a charge to Solomon follow, with lessons on work and worship. Through close Bible reading, MacLaren draws plain moral lessons for daily faith and duty.
79276-anthology-of-russian-literature-fr:
Leo Wiener made this gathering of Russian writing, from the earliest times to the present day, printed in New York and London. Wiener taught the Slavic tongues at Harvard. The work falls in two parts: from the tenth century to the close of the eighteenth, and the nineteenth century. This is the second part, of 1903. A picture of Turgenev stands at the front.

With it stand Turgenev's own words on his tongue: in days of doubt, he writes, you alone are my staff and stay, great and free Russian speech. Contents open with a sketch of Russian writing in the nineteenth century. Karamzin comes first, with his letters of a Russian traveller, Poor Liza, and the opening of his history of the Russian realm. Krylov follows with beast tales: the ass and the nightingale, the quartette, and the swan, the pike, and the crab.
7965-the-mahabharata-of-krishna-dwaipaya:
Book 2 of the Mahabharata, the Sabha Parva, appears here in Kisari Mohan Ganguli's English prose translation from the Sanskrit. The book takes its name from the sabha, the great assembly hall built for King Yudhishthira. And it follows his royal consecration, the gathering of kings, and the events that lead toward the fateful dice match. The translation was published between 1883 and 1896.

Ganguli's version made the Sanskrit epic available to English readers in full, and this volume shows why the work endures. Councils and ceremonies give way to pride, rivalry, and choices with terrible costs. The Sabha Parva is where the Pandavas' fortunes turn, setting up the exile and war that follow. It is essential reading for anyone approaching the epic in order.
9071-the-non-christian-cross-an-enquiry-:
John Denham Parsons published this inquiry in London in 1896. It asks where the cross, later the sign of the Christian faith, came from before Christ. Parsons began as a youth with four puzzles, such as why John the Baptist, beheaded before Jesus died, is shown holding a cross in art.

He traces the sign through old rites, baptism, and pagan use, arguing that Christians took up an older mark. The book is earnest and learned, if now dated in parts. It still interests readers who ask how symbols travel across faiths and ages.
9077-hamlet-the-first-bad-quarto:
This file gives an early printed text of Shakespeare's Hamlet, known as the first bad quarto. It was printed in 1603, before the fuller texts that followed. Scholars call it bad because it is short, rough, and differs in lines and scenes from the Hamlet we know. It may stem from actors' memories of the play.

The Gutenberg note warns that this is an early file, made when proof methods were weak. A better edition exists as ebook 100. Even so, this text fascinates students of Shakespeare, showing how a great play first reached print in a flawed, pirated form.
939-the-life-of-thomas-telford-civil-eng:
Samuel Smiles, the biographer of engineers, tells the life of Thomas Telford, the Scottish builder of roads, bridges, canals, and harbours. Telford rose from a shepherd's son to president of the Institution of Civil Engineers. Smiles wrote lives of engineers to inspire young men to industry and thrift.

Smiles follows Telford's works across Britain, from the Caledonian Canal to the Menai Bridge, praising industry and perseverance. The life remains a classic of Victorian biography, and a tribute to the men who built modern Britain. Telford's Menai suspension bridge, opened in 1826, was a wonder of its age.
a-complete-grammar-of-esperanto: Ivy Kellerman Reed gives a complete grammar of Esperanto for English speaking learners. The book presents the language not as a thing apart but as a stepping stone to national tongues. It explains Esperanto's special letters, including those with circumflexes and the breve, and Zamenhof's fallback spellings. Reed's grammar serves both beginners and teachers of the planned language.
a-little-princess-being-the-whole-story-:
Frances Hodgson Burnett wrote this children's novel about Sara Crewe, a pupil at Miss Minchin's London boarding school. A summary printed with the text tells the arc plainly: Sara is left in poverty when her father dies in India, then rescued by a mysterious benefactor. The contents list nineteen chapters, from her arrival as the school's pampered show pupil through the diamond mines excitement to her years in the attic.

As a servant girl, Sara keeps her manners, her stories, and her kindness to the scullery maid Becky and the rat she befriends. Next door lives a sickly Indian gentleman whose servant watches the attic child with growing interest. Burnett builds the ending on that wall between the houses. The book endures as a story about holding one's dignity when fortune turns.
anguttara-nikaya-sujato:
Bhikkhu Sujato translated the Anguttara Nikaya, the Numbered Discourses, in a complete modern version. The collection is the fourth great book of the Sutta Pitaka. It holds 1,313 discourses arranged in eleven books by number.

Ones come first: one vital quality that changes everything for practice. Twos, threes, and onward climb the ladder to elevens by the end. Three poisons, four noble truths, and five hindrances fit the scheme naturally. The arrangement served monks who memorized the teaching orally for centuries. Sujato's translation makes the vast memory-library easy to walk through. English readers can now browse the whole numbered system freely online.
around-the-world-on-a-bicycle-volume-i-f:
Thomas Stevens's Around the World on a Bicycle, volume one, rides from San Francisco to Teheran. The original edition, copyrighted in 1887, ran to 547 pages with over a hundred illustrations. Stevens crossed the Sierras in his first chapter on a high-wheel bicycle, the penny-farthing ordinary. He was the first man to circle the globe on a wheel.

America falls behind through Nevada deserts, Wyoming snow, and prairie towns that turned out to stare. Europe follows: England, France, Germany, and the Balkans in succession. Turkey and Persia end the volume at Teheran, where winter stopped the wheel. Stevens writes as a San Francisco journalist, wry about discomfort and curious about everything. Yogurt, caravanserais, and brigands enter his phonetic spellings. The book remains the classic of bicycle travel, half feat and half reportage.
britannica-1911-acciajuoli-donato:
Donato Acciajuoli (1428-1478) was an Italian scholar born at Florence, famous for his learning, especially in Greek and mathematics, and for service to his native city. Florence trusted him with several important embassies before making him Gonfalonier, its chief magistrate, in 1473. He died at Milan while travelling to Paris to ask Louis XI of France for aid against Pope Sixtus IV.

Honesty marked his public life. His body was buried at public expense, and Florence provided portions for his daughters because his probity had left the family little fortune. His writings include a Latin translation of some of Plutarch's Lives, commentaries on Aristotle's Ethics and Politics, and lives of Hannibal, Scipio, and Charlemagne.
britannica-1911-accolti-benedetto:
Benedetto Accolti (1415-1466) was an Italian jurist and historian born at Arezzo in Tuscany, of a noble family distinguished for attainments in law. He taught jurisprudence at the university of Florence, and when the celebrated Poggio died he became chancellor of the Florentine republic in 1459. He died at Florence, leaving works in both his fields.

History brought his widest influence. With his brother Leonardo he wrote a Latin history of the first crusade in three books, printed at Venice in 1432 and later translated into Italian and French. Though the entry calls it of little interest in itself, it is said to have given Tasso the historic basis for his epic Jerusalem Delivered. His brother Francesco was also a noted jurist.
britannica-1911-aibonito:
Cool air, not size, gave Aibonito its special role in Porto Rico. The inland town stands near 2,200 feet up. Its climate, free of malaria, led officials to pick it as a health station where foreign newcomers could adjust and the sick could recover. Aibonito heads a municipal district of the same name in the electoral district of Guayama.

The road from San Juan to Ponce runs through it, twenty-five miles east-north-east of Ponce. In 1899 the town counted 2,085 people and the district 8,596. Coffee farms ring the town, and fine tobacco grows close by. The great storm of August 1899 hit Aibonito hard and did much damage.
britannica-1911-albertinelli-mariotto:
Albertinelli, Mariotto, an Italian painter of 1474 to 1515, receives a brief entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born in Florence. His training tied his career to one partner above all, since he was a fellow-pupil of Fra Bartolommeo. The two became partners in their work, and many paintings came from their shared hand and shared workshop.

His chief paintings are in Florence, the city where he was born and trained. Among them one work stands out by name. The entry calls his Visitation of the Virgin, painted in 1503 and held at the Uffizi, his masterpiece. That picture shows the Virgin Mary visiting Elizabeth, a favourite subject of the period. Short as the notice is, it fixes the three facts by which Albertinelli is remembered: Florence, Fra Bartolommeo, and the Visitation of 1503.
britannica-1911-antonio-prior-of-crato:
Antonio, Prior of Crato, lived from 1531 to 1595 and claimed the throne of Portugal. The 1911 Britannica entry gives him as a natural son of Louis, duke of Beja. Schooled at Coimbra, he entered the order of Saint John and held the rich priory of Crato. Little is known of his life before the year 1578 in the record.

That year he sailed with King Sebastian on the invasion of Morocco in force. Moors captured him at Alcazar Kebir, where the king himself was slain in battle. A sly tale about his cross is said to have won him easy release. The entry opens the claim that would set Portugal and Spain at odds.
britannica-1911-arias-montano-benito:
Benito Arias Montano, a Spanish Bible scholar, is noted in a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in Estremadura in 1527, he learned at Seville and Alcalá. He took holy orders about the year 1559 in his prime. In 1562 the council of Trent took him as a church adviser. Two years on he withdrew to Peña de Aracena for quiet study.

His notes on the minor prophets came out in 1571 there. Philip the Second then sent him to Antwerp for a great task. There he shaped Plantin's polyglot Bible in eight vast tomes. That work came out across the years from 1568 to 1573. A Salamanca teacher charged him with heresy for that bold work. Rome heard his case and freed his name in full.
britannica-1911-ayuntamiento:
Ayuntamiento is the Spanish name for the district a town council governs, for the council itself, and for the town-hall. The word comes from Latin adjungere, and first meant a meeting. In parts of Spain and Spanish America the council was also called cabildo, from capitulum, a chapter.

Its members mixed officials with regidores, regulators drawn in varying shares from hidalgos, the nobles, and pecheros, commoners who paid the personal tax called pecho. A royal judge, the corregidor, checked the body and in fact chaired it for good. The noble and commoner split has vanished in modern Spain, the entry notes, while the councils' powers and make-up have changed many times.
britannica-1911-azuni-domenico-alberto:
Azuni, Domenico Alberto (1749-1827), was an Italian jurist born at Sassari in Sardinia, who studied law at Sassari and Turin and became judge of the consulate at Nice in 1782. His dictionary of mercantile law appeared in 1786-1788, the start of a career spent on the law of trade and the sea.

His systematic work on Europe's maritime law came in 1795 and was later recast in French. In 1806 France put him on the commission drafting a general commercial code, and he presided over Genoa's appeal court. After Napoleon's fall, Victor Emmanuel called him home to Sardinia as consulate judge and university library director at Cagliari, where he died. His other writings include a history of maritime law and an account of Sardinia itself.
britannica-1911-badalocchio-sisto:
Badalocchio, Sisto, surnamed Rosa (1581-1647), was an Italian painter and engraver born at Parma. He belonged to the school of Annibale Carracci, who esteemed him highly for design, his drawing. With Lanfranco, another Carracci pupil, he shared the craft that made his best-known work.

That work is the engraving series called Raphael's Bible, the pair's principal claim on memory. Badalocchio's paintings are few, and the best of them are at Parma, his birthplace. He died at Bologna in 1647. Painter, engraver, Carracci's valued pupil, and partner in a famous print series: those are the points this short entry fixes for a minor master of the Italian Baroque age.
britannica-1911-barquisimeto:
Barquisimeto is a city of western Venezuela, capital of the state of Lara, on the Barquisimeto river, 101 miles by rail south-west of its Caribbean port of Tucacas. Its population was estimated at 40,000 in 1899. It stands in a small fertile valley of the Merida Cordilleras, 1,985 feet above the sea, with a temperate, healthy climate.

Coffee, sugar, cacao, and rum come down from the rich country around it for export, and the city serves as a distributing centre for its neighbours. Founded in 1522 by Juan de Villegas and first called Nueva Segovia, it grew on trade to 15,000 people by 1807. An earthquake destroyed it wholly on 26 March 1812, killing 1,500. The 1911 Britannica entry notes its recovery as one of the few Venezuelan cities to regain its standing.
britannica-1911-baumgarten-crusius-ludwi:
Ludwig Friedrich Otto Baumgarten-Crusius (1788–1842), a German Protestant divine born at Merseburg, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He entered Leipzig university in 1805 to study theology and philology, the study of language and texts. After teaching there as a junior lecturer, he became a professor of theology at Jena in 1812. He stayed at Jena for life, rising to head its theological faculty.

Breadth gave his teaching its worth. Apart from church history, he lectured on nearly all of theoretical theology: New Testament exegesis, biblical theology, dogmatic ethics, and the history of dogma. His deep learning and wide sympathies are praised in the entry. His books include a textbook of Christian morals, grounds of biblical theology, and textbooks on the history of dogma. The last and best of these was left unfinished and was completed from his notes by Karl Hase in 1846.
britannica-1911-benevento:
Benevento is a town and archbishop’s see of Campania, Italy, capital of its province, sixty miles by rail north-east of Naples. It stands on a hill four hundred feet up, where the Calore and Sabbato rivers meet. In 1901 the town held 17,227 people and the commune 24,137.

The site is ancient Beneventum, first called Maleventum and said to be founded by Diomedes. Chief town of the Samnites, it served Rome as a base against Pyrrhus, took a Latin colony in 268 B.C., and kept its worth through the Punic and Social wars. Six main roads met there, and its medieval walls, near two miles long, follow the ancient line Totila razed in 542.
britannica-1911-bitonto:
Bitonto, in ancient times Butunti, is a town and episcopal see in Apulia, Italy. It lies in the province of Bari, ten miles west of Bari by steam tramway. Its population in 1901 was 30,617. The town was of no importance in classical times, the 1911 Britannica entry says plainly. Its medieval walls are still preserved. The cathedral is singled out as one of the finest works of Apulian Romanesque building. It has escaped damage from later restorations, the entry adds.

The palazzo Sylos-Labini holds a fine Renaissance court dated 1502. Those two buildings carry the whole account of the town. The entry runs to a short paragraph of a few lines. No trade, history, or events are recorded in its space. Walls, cathedral, and the one palace court are the picture it leaves. Bitonto stands here as a quiet cathedral town west of Bari.
britannica-1911-bonfigli-benedetto:
Benedetto Bonfigli was an Italian painter of the 1400s from Perugia. The entry opens with the state of Umbrian art in his day. Until near the middle of that century the Umbrian school lagged far behind Florence and the north. Then, with Perugino and his followers, it rose all at once into the first rank.

Among those followers, the entry says, none holds a higher place than Bonfigli. His chief surviving works are a series of frescoes telling the life of St Louis of Toulouse. They are painted in the communal palace of Perugia, his home city. The short account gives his standing in the school and this one great work, and little more.
britannica-1911-brin-benedetto:
Benedetto Brin (1833–1898) was an Italian naval administrator born at Turin on 17 May 1833 who worked as a naval engineer with distinction until he was forty. In 1873 Admiral Saint-Bon, minister of marine, made him under-secretary. The pair fitted well: Saint-Bon conceived a type of ship, Brin drew the plans and directed the building.

Made minister of marine in 1876, he carried Saint-Bon's programme further into the first full scheme for growing the Italian fleet. The huge warships Italia and Dandolo were his work, though he later dropped their type for smaller, faster ships of the Varese and Garibaldi class. Across eleven years as minister he raised a near-absent naval industry into large private shipyards, engine works and steel and gun plants. In 1892 he joined the Giolitti cabinet as foreign minister.
britannica-1911-buto:
Buto is the Greek name of an Egyptian goddess called Uto, treated in a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry. She was a cobra goddess of the marshes. Her chief city, also called Buto, lay in the north west of the Delta. A second place of that name lay to the north east.

The west city was the capital of the north kingdom in early times. So its goddess stood for Lower Egypt and the north. She is at times shown as a vulture, to match the vulture goddess of the south. More often she is a serpent wound round a papyrus stem. The Greeks linked her with Leto. Her temple, feast, and oracle are noted by Herodotus.
britannica-1911-casale-monferrato:
Casale Monferrato is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town and episcopal see of Piedmont, Italy, in the province of Alessandria. It lies in the plain on the right bank of the Po, 377 feet above sea level, 21 miles north north west of Alessandria by rail. The town counted 18,874 people in 1901, and its commune 31,370. Rail lines and steam tramways tie it to Mortara, Vercelli, Chivasso, and Asti.

The Lombard Romanesque cathedral, first founded in 742 and rebuilt in the early twelfth century, holds good pictures, and the church of S. Domenico is a fine Renaissance building. About ten miles away stands the Sacro Monte di Crea, with eighteen chapels of terra cotta statue groups on its slopes. Charlemagne gave the town to the church of Vercelli, and it won its liberty from Frederick Barbarossa. It was sacked in 1215, rebuilt and fortified in 1220, and passed under its marquises in 1292.
britannica-1911-castiglione-giovanni-ben:
Giovanni Benedetto Castiglione, an Italian painter who lived from 1616 to 1670, is profiled in a 1911 Britannica article. In Italy he was called Il Grechetto, and in France, Le Benédette. He belonged to the Genoese school. He was born in Genoa and studied for a time under Vandyck.

He painted portraits, scenes from history, and landscapes. He excelled most in fairs, markets, and rural scenes with animals. Noah and the animals entering the Ark was a pet subject of his. His paintings are found in Rome, Venice, Naples, and Florence. Genoa and Mantua hold the most of them. He also made a number of etchings. They are spirited, free, and full of taste, the text says. Diogenes searching for a Man is named as a chief one. His etchings, strong in light and shade, won him a fine name.
britannica-1911-cellini-benvenuto:
Benvenuto Cellini (1500–1571) is the subject of a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on an Italian artist, metal worker, and sculptor born in Florence. His father, Giovanni, made musical instruments and meant his son for the same trade. Benvenuto's bent for metal work proved stronger. At fifteen he was apprenticed to the goldsmith Antonio di Sandro, called Marcone. A street fray brought him six months of banishment to Siena.

After work in Siena and Bologna, Cellini reached Rome at nineteen. A silver casket, candlesticks, and a vase for the bishop of Salamanca brought him to the notice of Pope Clement VII. His gold medallion of Leda and the Swan won further fame. He also played the flute and joined the pope's court musicians. The entry turns next to his conduct in the attack on Rome by the constable de Bourbon in 1527. It praises his bravery and skill in that crisis.
britannica-1911-concerto:
Concerto, a music term in use from the start of the seventeenth century, is explained in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. At first the word had no fixed sense. It soon came to name works where unequal forces of voice or instruments are set against each other. The root points to striving or contest.

By the time of Bach the form stood firm as a work for instruments in many parts. Bach even used the word on the title pages of church cantatas. A mass of sound faces a smaller group, and the pull between them drives the music. In the concerto grosso that small group was called the concertino. Loud full passages trade places with split and varied groupings.
britannica-1911-contrafagotto:
Contrafagotto, or double bassoon, is a wood-wind instrument described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It plays the grand bass part for its family of double reed instruments. Its kin are the oboe, the cor anglais, and the bassoon. It stands to its family as the double bass stands to the strings, or the deep tuba to the brass.

Three makes of the instrument were in use in the day of the article. The modern German make keeps the shape of the bassoon. The best known is the work of Heckel, used at Bayreuth and in many German bands. Its wooden tube is more than sixteen feet long with a cone-shaped bore. The tube is bent back on itself four times to make it handy, so the whole is about as long as a bassoon. A small brass crook at the top holds the double reed.
britannica-1911-esparto:
Esparto, or Spanish grass, is a tough grass of Spain and north Africa, as a 1911 Britannica entry describes. It grows wild in the south of Spain and across the sea in Algeria. Dry, sunny, sandy ground by the coast suits it best of all soils. In Africa it goes by the names halfa or alfa in local speech.

The plant stands three or four feet high in clusters of stems. Young growth feeds cattle, but old stems gain great toughness of fibre. Pliny seems to describe the same plant as spartum in his natural history. Its long grey green leaves run from six inches to three feet in length.
britannica-1911-esperanto:
Esperanto is the subject of a 1911 Britannica entry on a made-up world tongue. It was first brought out in print in the year 1887. By 1911 it had fully pushed aside its forerunner, Volapuk. Its maker was a Russian doctor named Zamenhof, born in 1859.

He grew up at Bielostok, a town of four peoples and four tongues. Their feuds set him to dream of a neutral tongue for all. He saw that most words in a tongue are built from few roots. At first he tried to coin his roots from raw letters by rule. Then he took ready roots from the chief tongues of Europe. He drew them from more than one tongue, though not in even shares.
britannica-1911-espirito-santo:
Espirito Santo, a sea coast state of Brazil, is surveyed in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It is bound by Bahia, the Atlantic Ocean, Rio de Janeiro, and Minas Geraes. Its area is given as 17,316 square miles, the least of any state save Sergipe. Its count rose from 135,997 in 1890 to 209,783 in 1900.

The west is crossed by low hills that form the east edge of the high Brazil plain. The east is a low coast plain, much of it swamp and sand, but with rich soil in the north and south. Thick woods yield rosewood and other fine woods for export. Farm goods lead the trade, with sugar cane, coffee, rice, cotton, and fruit named first.
britannica-1911-fouche-joseph-duke-of-ot:
Joseph Fouche, duke of Otranto (1763-1820), French statesman, was born in a small village near Nantes on 21 May 1763. His father, a seafaring man, meant him for the sea, but his weak frame and quick talents changed the plan. He was educated at the college of the Oratorians at Nantes, showing strong gifts in literary and scientific studies alike. Sent to Paris to train as a teacher with the same order, he soon took up tutorial work in its colleges.

Fouche taught at Niort, Saumur, Vendome, Juilly and Arras, where he had dealings with Robespierre as the Revolution began. In October 1790 his order moved him back to Nantes. The long entry that follows traces the schoolmaster turned revolutionary. As minister of police under the Directory, Napoleon and the restored Bourbons, Fouche built the web of spies and files that made his name a byword for the police state in France.
britannica-1911-giusto-da-guanto:
Giusto da Guanto, Justus of Ghent (flourished 1465-1475), was a Flemish painter whose life the records barely show. The 1911 Britannica entry says Ghent's archives have been searched in vain for his history. Vasari and Guicciardini named him, and later Flemish writers made him a pupil of Hubert van Eyck, a claim the entry calls a fable.

His one secure work is the Communion of the Apostles, painted between 1465 and 1474 for a brotherhood at Urbino, now in that city's museum. Frederick of Montefeltro, who ordered it, appears in the picture beside a Persian envoy. The entry judges him a lesser composer and draughtsman than the great Flemings, though strong in portraits. It also weighs, without settling, whether he painted the series of ancient worthies at the Louvre and the Barberini palace.
britannica-1911-goito:
Goito is a village of Lombardy, Italy, in the province of Mantua, 11 miles north-west of that city on the road to Brescia. The 1911 Britannica entry gives the village 737 people and the commune 5,712. It stands on the right bank of the Mincio, near the bridge.

That position is the whole point of the notice. A bridge-head over the Mincio gave Goito military importance in campaign after campaign, and it was fortified again and again. The entry closes with two Piedmontese victories over the Austrians won there in 1848. The first fell on 8 April and the second on 30 May. The entry is a short place notice in which geography explains history: the river, the bridge, and the battles the crossing drew.
britannica-1911-kioto:
Kioto, the former capital of Japan, is described in an article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on a small river in the province of Yamashiro. Its people numbered 379,404 in 1903. A canal cut in 1890 linked it with Lake Biwa, bringing water for its factories and a through route by water toward Osaka. The city was founded in the year 793.

The article says Kioto stayed the capital of the empire for near eleven centuries. The emperor who chose the spot had the city laid out with strict order, on the model of a capital of the Tang line in China. Eighteen main streets crossed its ground, nine running north and south and nine east and west. Minor streets joined the two sets at intervals. The entry gives the plan of a court city drawn on a grid in a lovely setting.
britannica-1911-lista-y-aragon-alberto:
Alberto Lista y Aragon, who lived from 1775 to 1848, was a Spanish poet and teacher. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica opens with his birth at Seville. He began teaching at the age of fifteen. In his early twenties he held a chair of speech and poetry at Seville. Politics drove him into exile in 1813. A pardon let him come home four years later.

Back in Spain he taught at Bilbao and ran a review at Madrid. He then founded the San Mateo college in the capital. The state shut it in 1823 for its free bent. Years abroad in France and England followed. Called home in 1833, he edited the state gazette. He also helped found the Ateneo, a free seat of learning at Madrid. The entry stresses his reach as a teacher. A whole young crop of Spanish leaders learned under him.
britannica-1911-lotto:
Lotto is a gambling game of chance, known in America as keno. The 1911 Britannica article lays out how a game is played. Each player uses a large card split into three rows of nine spaces. Five spaces in each row carry numbers, and four stand blank. The numbers run up to ninety in all. A player may buy as many cards as he likes from the bank.

Ninety small balls, each with a number, are kept in a bag or in an urn with a spout. The banker draws them one by one and calls each number out loud. Players mark any number that shows on their cards. The first player to cover a full row calls out and takes the stakes. The bank keeps a fixed share of the pool as its cut.
britannica-1911-marcello-benedetto:
Benedetto Marcello, who lived from 1686 to 1739, was an Italian composer. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica weighs his psalms and satire. He came of a noble Venetian family. His father meant him for the law, not for music.

Marcello still sat on the Council of Forty in 1711. Ill health in a damp posting drove him to Brescia in time. His fame rests on a great set of fifty psalms in music. Those works, printed in the 1720s, won praise abroad. An English edition with new words came out in 1757. He also wrote a sharp satire on opera of his day. That small book, The Theatre in Fashion, still amuses readers. It also tells much about stage life then.
britannica-1911-montecristo: Montecristo is a brief island entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It names an island of Italy, in the province of Leghorn, south of Elba. Its old name was Oglasa. The island covers about six square miles, and its highest point stands 2,126 feet above the sea. Ruins of a monastery stand there, founded in the 1200s and wrecked in the 1500s. The island is the private land of the king of Italy. Its fame rests on a tale by the elder Dumas.
britannica-1911-oporto:
Oporto is the second city of Portugal and the chief town of the north. The 1911 Britannica entry places it on both banks of the river Douro. The stream meets the sea some three miles below the town. Its count in 1900 was 167,955 souls, a large port town. The part south of the river bears the name Villa Nova de Gaia.

In strict Portuguese use the name should be written Porto. Long use in English fixed the form Oporto all the same. The town is the seat of a bishop in the province of Braga. Three main rail lines meet there and link it to the frontiers. Trade and public life make it the true rival of Lisbon.
britannica-1911-perez-galdos-benito:
Benito Pérez Galdós, a Spanish novelist born in 1845, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Las Palmas in the Canary Islands. In 1863 he was sent to Madrid to read law, but slid into letters. He was soon marked as a bright new name on the Liberal side.

After the revolution of 1868 he left journalism and made the novel his tool. His grand scheme was a chain of tales of the recent past of Spain. He stocked his mind with old charters, letters, and news sheets like a keeper of records. The first chain of ten books ran from 1879 to 1881 and made his name. A second and third chain raised the count to forty volumes. The entry sets his rich yield of work beside that of Balzac.
britannica-1911-philemon-epistle-to:
Epistle to Philemon is a short book of the New Testament, treated in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Onesimus, a slave, had robbed his master Philemon and run away from him. Philemon was a rich and well placed Christian of Colossae. Onesimus met Paul, who won him to the Christian faith. Paul then sent him back with a brief, kind note.

In that note Paul greets Philemon, his wife, and the church that met in his house. He praises the faith and love of his friend at some length. He then pleads for kind treatment of Onesimus, now a true convert. The slave was to take his place in the house once more. The text weighs where Paul wrote the note, Rome or Caesarea, and leans to Rome. Links with the letters to the Colossians and to the Philippians are also weighed.
britannica-1911-pimento:
Pimento, also called allspice and Jamaica pepper, is the dried unripe fruit of a West Indian tree. The tree is an evergreen of the myrtle order, about thirty feet high. It is native to the West India Islands and grows on limestone hills near the sea. It is grown above all in Jamaica. The name allspice comes from a fancied blend of many tastes in one spice.

The berries are picked in July and August, when full grown but still unripe. The small branches that bear fruit are broken off and dried in sun and air for some days. The stalks are then stripped away and the berries are fit for packing. Their scent and bite come from a rich oil in the fruit. The chief use of pimento is as a spice in food.
britannica-1911-pinto:
Pinto is a skin disease marked by brown, black, and blue spots over the whole body. A 1911 Britannica medical entry places it in Mexico, Panama, Colombia, and Venezuela. One writer in 1881 held that a plant like parasite caused the spots. Its threads were said to show among deep cells of the skin.

The entry links the disease to want and poor living, yet notes it can spread by contact. In some villages in Tabasco in Mexico near one person in eleven had it. A visitor in 1826 saw a whole regiment of marked men in Mexico City. Readers get a clear sense of how wide and strange the ill was thought to be.
britannica-1911-pluto:
The 1911 Britannica article on Pluto treats the Greek god of the lower world. His oldest name was Hades, the Unseen. He was a son of Cronus and Rhea. He was a brother of Zeus and Poseidon. The three brothers drew lots for the realms. The world below fell to Pluto.

There he ruled with his wife Persephone. He was stern and pitiless. Prayer and sacrifice could not move him. Only the music of Orpheus won back a dead wife. His helmet made him unseen. Men feared to speak his name. They used kinder titles instead. Later belief softened him into a giver of grain and wealth. The Romans called him Dis Pater and Orcus. His signs were a sceptre and the hound Cerberus.
britannica-1911-ribbeck-johann-carl-otto:
Johann Carl Otto Ribbeck, a German scholar of the Latin and Greek classics, is profiled in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. He was born at Erfurt in 1827. He held chairs at Kiel and at Heidelberg. He then took the chair of classical studies at Leipzig that his own tutor Ritschl had held, and died there in 1898.

The entry lists his chief works on the poets of Rome. They cover the growth of Roman verse, Roman tragedy, and the scraps of lost plays. As a shaper of old texts he was bold to a fault in his youth. He would shift, cut, or drop lines that fell short of his mark. In later years he grew more careful. His edition of Virgil is praised for its vast learning.
britannica-1911-rio-cuarto:
Rio Cuarto is a town of Argentina in the province of Cordoba, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes its site and trade. It stands on the open plain halfway across the great pampas, 1,440 feet above the sea, on a river of the same name. The town lies south of the city of Cordoba and far north-west of Buenos Aires. Its people were put at about twelve thousand in 1904, and pleasant suburbs ring the town.

Rio Cuarto is the trade centre of a large district and does a rich business. Its place on the map gives it weight in war, and the government keeps a large arsenal and a garrison of the regular army there. The country round belongs to the drier pampa and is given to raising cattle, horses, sheep, and goats, with watering used near the town.
britannica-1911-rio-tinto:
Rio Tinto is a mining town in south western Spain, in Huelva province. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica sets it near the source of the Tinto river. Copper in its waters gives the river its tinted name, it says. More than ten thousand miners lived in the town and nearby villages.

The site ranks among the great copper centers of the world. In 1903 its mines yielded 840000 tons of copper ore for export. Most ore went to Huelva for shipment to Britain by sea. Carthaginians likely worked the mines first, with Roman traces still seen. A London and Bremen group bought them in 1872 for near four million pounds.
britannica-1911-rodosto:
Rodosto, called Tekir Dagh in Turkish, is a town of European Turkey described in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. It stands on the coast of the Sea of Marmora, west of Constantinople. In 1905 it held about thirty-five thousand people, half of them Greeks. A high headland wraps its fine bay on one side.

The town was long a great store port for the Adrianople district. Its trade fell when a rail line up the Maritza ended at another port. Grain, seed, and goods by sea now bear its trade. Mulberry trees feed silk worms round the town, and white cocoons go west to Europe. In a church there lie Hungarians exiled in 1686, with long Latin texts on their graves. The town is the old Rhaedestus, sacked twice by the Bulgarians.
britannica-1911-rovereto:
Rovereto is a 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica entry on a town in Tirol. It is the most important industrial town in the south of that province. That southern part is Italian speaking in character. Its people in 1900 numbered 10,180 in all. They were Italian speaking and Roman Catholic. It is the chief town of its own administrative district. It is built on the left bank of the Adige.

The town stands in the widest part of the Val Lagarina. The Leno torrent divides the town into two parts. It sits on the Brenner railway south west of Trent. Save in the newer quarter, its streets are narrow and crooked. Several streets bear the name of Antonio Rosmini-Serbati. He was the most distinguished native of the place. The finest church is Santa Maria del Carmine.
britannica-1911-soleto: Soleto is a village of Apulia in south Italy, in the province of Lecce. The 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica places it eleven miles south of Lecce by rail. It stands 299 feet above sea level and held 3,349 people in 1901. Its Romanesque church of St Stefano holds wall paintings in the Greek style from the fourteenth century. Those paintings match work in cave chapels near Vaste, south of Otranto. A rich bell tower beside the old cathedral dates from 1397.
britannica-1911-sorrento:
Sorrento is a place article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a city of Campania in Italy. Sorrento stands on cliffs about 160 feet above the sea. It sits on the peninsula that parts the Bay of Naples from the Bay of Salerno. Its population in 1901 was 6,849 in the town and 8,832 in the commune. The article says the town holds few ancient remains.

Its prosperity rests on its name as a resort in winter and summer alike. In 1558 the corsair Pialy attacked the town and carried off two thousand prisoners. Its poets are Bernardo Tasso, who wrote his Amadigi here, and his son Torquato, born in the town in 1544.
britannica-1911-sweet-potato:
Sweet Potato is a plant article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a climbing plant grown across the tropics for its root. Its plant name is Ipomaea batatas, and it belongs to the same family as bindweed. Its leaves vary much in shape, and its flowers are white or rosy funnels on long stalks. The part men eat is the root.

The root swells into large club-shaped masses full of starch. The plant will not thrive in the British climate, but in warm lands it is worth as much as the potato is in cooler ones. No one knows it in a truly wild state, and its home is not sure. The writer cited, de Candolle, holds that it most likely came from America. There it had been grown since before written history by the native peoples.
britannica-1911-tasso-torquato:
Torquato Tasso (1544–1595) was an Italian poet, son of Bernardo Tasso, a noble of Bergamo. His mother was Porzia de' Rossi, of a famed family of Naples. He was born at Sorrento on 11 March 1544. His father had long been a secretary to the prince of Salerno. That prince fell out with the Spanish rule of Naples and was cast out and stripped of his lands. Tasso's father shared in that fall.

Bernardo was named a rebel to the state, with his son Torquato, and his wealth was seized. All this fell in the boy's young years. In 1552 the boy lived at Naples with his mother and his one sister, Cornelia. He was schooled by the Jesuits, who had just opened a school there. His quick mind and his deep faith at that age drew the praise of all.
britannica-1911-timothy-second-epistle-t:
Timothy, Second Epistle to is a Bible article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a book of the New Testament. After thanks for Timothy's faith, Paul warns him against false shame. Endurance is urged, and Timothy is told to hold to the Pauline gospel. A solemn charge to faithfulness follows, and a note of personal matters closes the letter.

The article then argues that the letter was not written as it stands by Paul. Its last verse, with a two-fold greeting, shows it was meant for a wider circle than Timothy alone. Its origin is composite: the personal note is genuine Paul, yet its parts clash. A later writer worked Paul's real notes into a letter in his name.
britannica-1911-tomato:
Tomato is a 1911 Britannica article on a garden plant and how to raise it. The tomato is a tender annual. It is native to South America, most likely Peru. It belongs to the family Solanaceae. Its fruit is much esteemed in salads and as a vegetable.

Plants meant to fruit out of doors in summer need an early start. Seed should be sown at the end of February, or early in March, under glass. Pots, pans, or shallow boxes suit the purpose. The compost should be light and fresh. Loam, sand, and leaf mould in equal shares are preferred. As soon as the young plants appear, they need full sunlight. They should stand as near the glass as can be managed. When the second pair of leaves appears, the plants should be potted on. Garden readers get a season plan from seed to setting out.
britannica-1911-toronto:
Toronto is the capital of the province of Ontario and the second largest city in Canada, as this 1911 Britannica article presents it. It stands on the north shore of Lake Ontario, on a plateau rising from the lake to about 220 feet, and covers nearly twenty square miles. The river Don flows through its east part, and the Humber forms its west limit.

A bay in front of the city gives a safe harbour, sheltered by an island. The streets cross at right angles, and Yonge Street, the chief road, runs north from the bay toward Lake Simcoe. The article notes the parliament buildings in Queen's Park, built of red sandstone, and the nearby university buildings set round a broad campus.
britannica-1911-trevelyan-sir-george-ott:
Sir George Otto Trevelyan, author and statesman, opens a life in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. Born in 1838 at Rothley Temple, he was an only son. His mother was a sister of Lord Macaulay, the famed writer. At Harrow and Trinity College, Cambridge, he shone in classics. He stood second in the great classical exam of his year there.

A verse play of his youth may have cost him a fellowship. In 1862 he went to India as a civil servant. His sprightly letters from India ran in a London magazine. His book Cawnpore told the grim tale of that siege. In 1865 he won a seat in parliament for Tynemouth. He pushed army reform and a wider vote for county homes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-andrea-del-sa:
Andrea del Sarto, born Andrea d'Agnolo at Florence in 1486, dead there in 1531, took his surname from his tailor father. He studied first under the obscure G. Barile, then from 1498 in Piero di Cosimo's studio. He visited Rome briefly. Vasari says that, had he stayed to study its masterpieces, he would have surpassed every artist of his day. Diffident, he felt a stranger there and hurried back to Florence.

Despite his short career he produced many frescoes and easel pictures. From 1509 he decorated the Annunziata cloister for the Servites, with five scenes from Saint Philip Benizi's life and, in 1525, the Madonna of the Sack. In 1514 he began ten frescoes in the cloister of the Scalzo. Later works include the Madonna of the Harpies at the Uffizi, a Virgin with Saints at Berlin, and a Pieta at Vienna. Francis I bought two of them and drew him to Paris.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-atto:
Atto, probably born at Milan, was a faithful backer of Pope Gregory VII in his fight against simoniac clergy, priests who bought church office. He was made Cardinal of San Marco. He stood by at the retractation of Berengarius at the Roman synod of 1079, and signed the decrees of the synod of 1081. He may also have served as Bishop of Praeneste, though the entry leaves that point open.

Cardinal Mai later published, under Atto's name and from a Vatican manuscript, a Breviarium Canonum. It is a mixed store of moral and church-law decrees, genuine and forged, running from Pope Clement I to Gregory the Great. It deals in particular with clerical rights and duties, church acts, the sacraments, censures, and jurisdiction. The entry closes by noting other cardinals of the same name, discussed in an anonymous eighteenth-century tract on the Attos.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-barquisimeto:
Barquisimeto is a diocese in Venezuela, its city the capital of Lara State, about 161 miles southwest of Caracas. Founded by Spaniards in 1552 as Nueva Segovia, it ranks among South America's oldest Spanish possessions. An 1812 earthquake almost entirely destroyed it, and its population runs about 30,000, though some authorities give less.

The diocese was erected in 1847 over Lara, Carabobo, and Falcon. By a 1907 decree, the bishop's residence moved to Valencia, and the boundaries were rearranged. It now meets the Caribbean on the north and west, Mérida to the south, and Calabozo, Zamora, and Guiana to the east. It counts 528,215 Catholics, 68 priests, and 110 churches and chapels.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-benevento:
Benevento, an ancient city of Campania in southern Italy, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Founded by the Samnites as Maleventum, it passed to Rome after the defeat of Pyrrhus in 275 BC and took its present name. A Roman colony followed, enlarged by Augustus, whose age is recalled by the marble arch of Trajan still standing.
