Medieval and modern turns fill the rest: capture by Totila, Norman fealty to Pope Leo IX, centuries as papal territory, and annexation to the Kingdom of Italy in 1860. The future Pope Leo XIII served there as papal delegate. The entry closes with its archdiocese, its suffragan sees, and its native popes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-bl-john-de-br:
Blessed John de Britto, a Jesuit martyr in India, is the subject of this 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia entry. Born in Lisbon in 1647 and raised at court, he was martyred in India in 1693. Joining the Jesuits at fifteen, he chose Madura in southern India as his field, reaching Goa in September 1673.

After thirty days of Ignatian retreat near Cranganore, he entered the Kshatriya caste's world in dress and diet, wearing yellow cotton and eating no meat or wine. On foot across the Ghats he reached the Cauvery delta and mastered the local language. Arrest for preaching ended in martyrdom. The entry presents a courtier turned Indian missionary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-casale-monfer:
Casale Monferrato is a diocese suffragan to Vercelli, set in Alessandria province in Piedmont on the River Po. The ancient Bodincomagus, it has been a stronghold since Lombard times. King Liutprand enlarged it, and Otto II made it a marquisate town for the sons of Aleran, Duke of Saxony. It later passed to the Palaeologi, then in 1533 to the Gonzaga, to France from 1681 to 1706, and to Savoy in 1713.

Sixtus IV created the see in 1474, after it belonged to Asti, with Bernardino de Tebaldeschi as first bishop. His successor Gian Giorgio Paleologo also governed the marquisate for a minor nephew. Notable bishops include Benedetto Erba, zealous for children's instruction and Tridentine reform beside Charles Borromeo. Giulio Careta founded a priests' oratory and nursed plague victims in 1630. The diocese counts 200,500 people in 140 parishes, with a cathedral ranked among the finest Lombard monuments.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-civitavecchia:
Civitavecchia, an important fortified Mediterranean seaport in Rome province, keeps fortifications and piers dating from Emperor Trajan. Popes from Eugene the Fourth to Urban the Eighth improved it under their temporal rule. Pope Cornelius was exiled to Centumcellae, the city's ancient name, during the Gallus persecution, and catacombs have been found there. Epictetus, its bishop, attended the Council of Arles in 314, while a later Epictetus, a rabid Arian, counselled Emperor Constantius badly.

The see was suppressed in 1086 and joined first to Toscanella, then in 1193 to Viterbo. Leo the Twelfth restored it in 1825 with Porto and Santa Rufina, and in 1854 it was united instead with Corneto. Corneto, near the ruins of Tarquinii, once capital of southern Etruria, shows its advanced civilisation in painted pottery from its many tombs. Its Christianity came not from Rome or by sea but from neighbouring Bolsena. The diocese counts 29,700 Catholics in twelve parishes.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-dominic-soto:
Dominic Soto was a Dominican theologian born at Segovia in 1494 who died at Salamanca in 1560. He studied first at home, then at Alcala under Saint Thomas of Villanova, and later at Paris, where he took a degree in philosophy. A Catholic Encyclopedia entry tells how he returned to Alcala about 1520 as professor of philosophy at San Ildefonso. There he won a full triumph for moderate realism over the errors of nominalism.

Already famed as a teacher, he gave up his chair in 1524 for the religious life, retreating first to Montserrat. His commentaries on the Sentences and on Romans, printed at Salamanca and Antwerp, kept his name alive in the schools. The entry cites Echard and Hurter among the sources for a career cut between the lecture hall and the cloister.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-fernao-mendes:
Fernao Mendes Pinto was a Portuguese traveller and classic prose writer of the East. Born about 1509, he sailed to the East Indies in 1537. For twenty-one years he wandered the Far East by sea. Shipwrecked and enslaved at times, he survived to tell his tale.

Pinto first told Europe of Japan's riches and built the first settlement near Yokohama in 1548. His Peregrinacao, printed in 1614, became a Portuguese classic. Some call it romance, but its substantial honesty is now generally admitted. He wrote from memory, setting down vivid impressions rather than bare facts.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-filipo-archin:
Filipo Archinto was an Italian theologian, diplomatist, and churchman. Born at Milan in 1500, he took his law doctorate at Padua at twenty. Paul III made him governor of the City of Rome and vice-chamberlain apostolic. He became bishop of the Holy Sepulchre and later of Saluzzo.

Archinto presided at Trent for the pope before the council's transfer to Bologna. St Ignatius gained a powerful protector in him in the Society's early years. Paul IV named him for Milan's archbishopric, but death prevented his installation. His theological works include De fide et sacramentis of 1545.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-batt:
Giovanni Battista Salvi da Sassoferrato was a painter born at Sassoferrato in 1609, who died at Rome in 1689, where he spent most of his life. His father Tarquinio taught him first, and at Naples he studied under Domenichino and through him the Carracci. A Catholic Encyclopedia article presents a painter of Madonnas whose tender sweetness rivaled Carlo Dolci.

Where many seventeenth-century Virgins look cold and distant from the Child, his Madonnas show a mother's heart, with a pleasing intimacy and naiveté. His masterpiece, Our Lady of the Rosary with St. Dominic and St. Catherine, was painted for the Princess de Rossano. Finished in 1643, it hangs in St. Sabina in Rome. His Madonnas fill museums from London and Paris to St. Petersburg and Vienna.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-giovanni-cler:
Giovanni Clericato was a canonist born at Padua in 1633, who died in 1717. Of English descent, his family name, written in several forms, probably came from Clark. The charity of a pious woman let him follow his strong bent for study. Raised to the priesthood, he came to rank among the ablest men of his time in ecclesiastical jurisprudence. A Catholic Encyclopedia article holds his name in honor in Italian church literature.

Cardinal Barbarigo, whose life Clericato later wrote, named him vicar-general for Padua. His many works on civil and canon law include Decisiones Sacramentales, published in 1727 and again in three volumes in 1757, which won the praise of Benedict XIV. Those books kept his name alive among canon lawyers.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-grosseto:
Grosseto, a suffragan diocese of Siena, takes its name from the Tuscan town at the mouth of the Ombrone river in the unhealthy Maremma country. Its story starts in 803, when the Aldobrandeschi counts held it as a fief, it grew as older Rusellae and Vetulonia decayed and passed to Sienese control in 1224. It kept its fortress walls and bastions as marks of its time as a stronghold.

Its church story runs from Rusellae, an episcopal city from the fifth century, to the transfer of the see to Grosseto by Innocent II in 1138. The Romanesque cathedral, finished in 1295 with a striped marble front, anchors a roll of bishops that includes a Trent figure, Marcantonio Campeggio. The entry closes with 26 parishes and 30,250 faithful.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-gugliemo-sirl:
Calabrian scholar Guglielmo Sirleto, born at Guardavalle in 1514, became one of the Council of Trent's most trusted behind-the-scenes minds. A friend of Marcello Cervino, later Marcellus II, he wrote full reports on the council's questions, catalogued the Vatican Library's Greek manuscripts, and brought out a fresh Vulgate edition.

Made cardinal in 1565 and Vatican librarian in 1570, he steered the scientific work Trent had ordered: the Roman Catechism, the reform of Breviary and Missal, and a new Roman Martyrology. A lover of Greek culture who encouraged reunion with the East, he taught Greek and Hebrew at Rome, counting St. Charles Borromeo among his pupils, and died attended by St. Philip Neri.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-haito:
Basle's Bishop Haito, born of a Swabian noble family in 763, entered Reichenau at five, headed its school under Abbot Waldo, and became abbot and bishop together about 806. Trusted by Charlemagne, he carried a diplomatic mission to Constantinople in 811 and rebuilt the cathedrals of Basle and Reichenau. He issued guidance for clergy and people before resigning both offices in 823 through infirmity.

His writings include a lost account of the Constantinople journey and the Visio Wettini of 824, in which the dying schoolmaster Wettin tours hell, purgatory, and heaven under an angel's guidance. That vision was later versified by Walafrid Strabo, and the Capitulare Haitonis, twenty-five chapters of diocesan discipline, was probably issued at a synod.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hatto:
Mainz Archbishop Hatto, born of a Swabian noble family about 850, was monk, abbot, and kingmaker in a Germany pulling toward fragmentation. Educated at Ellwangen, a Benedictine at Fulda, abbot of Reichenau in 888 and Ellwangen a year later, he won King Arnulf's trust and the archbishopric of Mainz in September 891.

His guiding aim was a united German kingdom under a strong king. This made dukes who wanted independent states hate him. After Arnulf's death he steered the election of the six-year-old Louis the Child and governed during his short reign. He then secured Conrad I of Franconia as king and served as his chief counsellor until his death in 913. He has been maligned ever since by tales of treachery and the mouse-tower fable, both without foundation.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-hernando-de-s:
Hernando de Soto was a Spanish explorer and conqueror, born in Extremadura around 1496 or 1500 and dead on the banks of the Mississippi in June 1542. He served in Central America, joined Pizarro's conquest of Peru as second in command, and became the first Spaniard to speak with the Inca Atahualpa. He grew disgusted when Pizarro had Atahualpa killed despite a large ransom.

De Soto then won the governorship of Cuba and leave to conquer Florida. He sailed in 1538, rebuilt Havana, and marched north through the American southeast with hundreds of horses, seeking riches and a route to New Spain. He died of fever before reaching it, and his men hid his body in the great river. The entry traces a career of bold marches, harsh clashes, and a quest that outran its leader.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ignacio-de-ar:
Ignacio de Arbieto was a Jesuit, born at Madrid in February 1585 and dead at Lima in 1670. He entered the Society of Jesus in 1603, and Lima saw his priestly ordination in 1612. Quito in Ecuador gave him its philosophy chair first; Arequipa came next, and Lima last, where he died.

Over twenty-five interrupted years he taught in Peru, then gave his final years to a History of Peru and its Jesuit foundations. That manuscript lies at Lima's National Archives in a hopeless state of decay. The entry preserves what is known of a scholar-teacher whose chief work survives only as a crumbling manuscript.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-il-tintoretto:
Jacopo Robusti, called Il Tintoretto or the little dyer, was a Venetian painter born in 1518 and dead there in 1594. His father dyed cloth, which explains the nickname. Young Jacopo played the harp well, yet painting drew him even more. His parents placed him with old Titian as an apprentice, but the ambitious youth soon opened his own studio.

He aimed to remake Venetian painting altogether. He kept its brilliant, harmonious colour and graceful forms, and joined to them Florentine and Roman strengths: anatomy strong in the nude, dramatic staging, moving poses, and bold light-and-shade contrasts. Ridolfi, his biographer, sums up the program as Michelangelo's drawing wedded to Titian's colouring.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-in-petto:
Reserved “in the breast” is the plain sense of this Italian phrase, used when a pope names cardinals in secret. At a consistory, the formal meeting where cardinals are created, a pope may add that he is holding back one or more names to reveal later. This entry explains what that secret naming did and did not do.

Until their names were made public, cardinals kept in petto held no rights of office. If the pope died first they never joined the Sacred College. Once proclaimed at a later consistory, they ranked from the date of their first naming and drew pay from that date. Popes used the device at times to secure a living for poor churchmen facing the costs of promotion.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jacopo-sadole:
Cardinal Jacopo Sadoleto was a humanist and reformer born at Modena in 1477. He died at Rome in 1547. His father, a noted lawyer, meant him for law. Jacopo instead pursued classical and philosophical studies. At Rome he won favor from Cardinal Caraffa and later from Leo X. Leo made him his secretary. In 1517 he became bishop of Carpentras near Avignon.

Unlike many humanists, he lived a blameless life. He attended closely to his duties as priest and bishop. Only at popes' express command would he leave his diocese even briefly. He combined piety, letters, and action in high degree. As poet, orator, theologian, and philosopher he ranked foremost in his age. His poem on the newly found Laocoön first drew learned notice. The entry presents a humanist who stayed a pastor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lepanto:
Lepanto is the Italian name for Naupactos, a titular metropolitan see of ancient Epirus. Naupactus means dockyard, from the Heraclidae fleet tale. Athens took it from the Locri Ozolae and in 455 B.C., after the Third Messenian War, settled there the Messenian helots, Sparta's bitter enemies. After Aegospotami in 404 B.C. Sparta seized the town, drove out the Messenians, and gave it back to the Locri.

It then passed through Achaean, Thespian, and Macedonian hands to the Aetolians. Naupactus resisted Rome fiercely for two months before M. Acilius Glabrio took it in 191 B.C. An earthquake nearly destroyed it under Justinian. Its first known Greek bishop sat at Ephesus in 431. The see depended on the pope until Leo III annexed it to Constantinople in 733. It joined the Greek Orthodox Church in 1827 and was suppressed in 1900 for the See of Acarnania and Naupactia at Missolonghi.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-litany-of-lor:
The Litany of Loreto is a Marian prayer, a set of short appeals to Mary answered in turn by those praying. It took its name from the shrine at Loreto in Italy, where pilgrims learned it and carried it home across Europe.

Its roots are murky, and the entry weighs rival claims that push it back to the early Church. Sound evidence points instead to the late fifteenth or early sixteenth century. The oldest printed copy found so far comes from Dillingen in 1558, and Church approval followed in 1587. Later parts trace its set form, its spread, and its many titles for Mary.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-lorenzo-lotto:
Lorenzo Lotto was an Italian portrait painter, born at Venice in 1480 and dead at Loreto in 1556. He ranks among the finest portraitists who ever lived, prized for catching the quirks of a sitter's character and matching them to mood and temper.

A great colourist with a mystical bent, he spent his last years at Loreto in devotion to its Holy House. Early work took him to Treviso, Recanati, and Rome, where Raphael's art marked his paintings of 1512 to 1525. Bergamo claims him most, though his finest pictures also grace small towns like Jesi, Cingoli, and Trescorre, and his account book from 1539 tracks his late output.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ludovico-ario:
Ludovico Ariosto, called the Italian Homer, was a Ferrarese poet, born at Reggio in 1474 and dead at Ferrara in 1533. Eldest of ten, he headed his family after his father's death in 1500, having written and acted a fable at nine and studied law five years before turning to Greek and Latin.

Courtier to Cardinal Ippolito d'Este from about 1503, then diplomat for Duke Alfonso, he governed bandit-ridden Garfagnana from 1522 to 1525. His glory rests on Orlando Furioso, begun about 1505 and published in 1516, then enlarged in 1532. Paris besieged, Orlando's rage, and Ruggiero's love for Bradamante, founding the Este line, spin its dazzling web of adventures.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-luni-sarzana-:
Luni-Sarzana-Brugnato is a diocese in Genoa province, joining three histories. Luni, first Etruscan, then Ligurian, then Roman, gave its port, modern Spezia, and its marble, now Carrara marble, to antiquity. Vandals, Lombards, and Saracens sacked it, and its people moved to Sarzana in 1058.

Sarzana, first named in 963, held bishops' rule contested by Malaspina marquesses, Pisans, and Genoese. It hosted a congress of Italian princes in 1353, and keeps walls, a citadel, and a cathedral from after 1200. Brugnato's smaller story, with its own bishops and churches, completes a diocese of ruins, relics, and stubborn survival.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-mileto:
Mileto, a Calabrian city in the province of Reggio in southern Italy, was founded, so tradition holds, not far from ancient Medama. Tradition says fugitives from Miletus in Asia Minor, a town Darius had destroyed, founded it. It bore the brunt of many earthquakes, above all those of 1905 and 1906, and in lesser measure the 28 December 1908 shock that laid waste to Reggio and Messina.

Gregory VII made Mileto an episcopal see in 1073. Count Roger had raised its cathedral, and the 1783 earthquake wrecked it. He had also set up a house for Greek Basilian monks, the monastery of the Most Holy Trinity and St. Michael. Callistus II later joined its diocese to those of Tauriana and Vibona. Mileto's Norman roots and its long line of bishops mark it among Calabria's historic sees.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-montalto:
Montalto is a little town in Ascoli Piceno whose attractive setting first fell under the abbots of Farfa in 1074, then passed in 1571 to the Diocese of Ripatransone under Pius V. Its fortunes changed when a native son rose to the papacy.

Sixtus V, born at Montalto, made it a bishop's see in 1586, with Paolo Emilio Giovannini as its first bishop. Later bishops included Orazio Giustiniani, who became a cardinal in 1640, and Francesco Saverio Castiglioni, who took office in 1800 and later reigned as Pius VII. The diocese counts 33 parishes and 29,000 people, served by 79 secular and 4 regular priests, with one house of men religious and one of sisters.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-noto:
Noto, a Sicilian diocese separated from Syracuse in 1844, rose from an ancient city rebuilt after disaster. Ancient Netum, later capital of a Saracen division of Sicily, held out late against the Normans and was destroyed by earthquake in 1693, then rebuilt nearly five miles from its old site.

Fine churches, a museum holding Syracusan, Roman, and Saracen coins, plus a library mark the new town, birthplace of the humanist John Aurispa. Its cathedral holds the tomb of Blessed Conrad of Piacenza, and the diocese counts 19 parishes and 148,400 people. Its first bishop was Joseph Menditto, after separation from Syracuse in 1844.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-oporto:
Oporto, a Portuguese diocese of twenty-six concelhos in Oporto and Aveiro, likely dates from the mid-sixth century. At Toledo's third council in 589 the Arian usurper Argiovito fell for Constancio, and bishops appear at Toledo and Braga councils through the Visigothic age.

After Arab conquest, Justus led the see, Gomado followed Alfonso III's recovery in 872, and Hugo, bishop from 1114, won exemption from Braga and enlarged cathedral lands. The entry carries Oporto's bishops, churches, and wine trade through medieval and modern centuries. Bishop Froarico attended councils at Braga and Toledo through the 680s.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-orvieto:
Orvieto is a diocese in central Italy whose city crowns a rugged mass of tufa rock near the Paglia and Chiana rivers. Some link the town with ancient Hebanum. Others hold it was the old port, Urbs Vetus, of the Etruscan city of Volsinii, destroyed by Rome and rebuilt at Bolsena. Etruscan tombs ring the country round, and the name Urbs Vetus first shows in Procopius.

Defended by Goths in the Gothic War, the city was taken by Lombards in 606. It later ran itself through consuls, then a podesta and a captain of the people from 1201. It often sheltered popes in flight. Its great cathedral, its relic of the Bolsena miracle, and its line of bishops fill the later pages. A frank note adds that the miracle tale rests on weak and uneven evidence.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-otranto:
Otranto is an archdiocese and city of Lecce province in Apulia, southern Italy, set in fertile country once famed for its horses. An ancient Greek colony, it stood against Rome in the wars of Pyrrhus and Hannibal. As the nearest port to the Adriatic's eastern shore, it outranked Brindisi under the Roman emperors. It passed through Beneventan and Byzantine hands, and was among the last Apulian cities to yield to Robert Guiscard in 1068.

In 1480 Turks sacked the city, and 12,000 men are said to have died, among them Bishop Stephen Pendinelli, sawn to death, while later Turkish landings in 1537 were beaten off. Napoleon gave Otranto in fief to Fouche in 1810, after a French garrison lodged there from 1804. Its cathedral, built by Count Roger I in 1088, bears a mosaic floor of about 1163, and a Basilian house there grew into a place of study under Abbot Nicetas.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-paolo-farinat:
Paolo Farinato was an Italian painter born at Verona in 1524 and dead there in 1606. He sprang from the old Florentine house of Farinata degli Uberti, the Ghibelline chief Dante placed in his Inferno. When the Guelfs won, the Uberti were expelled, and one branch settled at Verona. Paolo learned under Giolfino, heir to the miniature tradition of Liberale, famed for choir-book pictures at Siena.

Verona, a town without a great artistic past, thus bred a fresh school, free to try novel colour schemes already seen in the tombs of Cane Grande della Scala. Late in the fifteenth century, Bellini, Giorgione, and Titian brought an artistic revolution to the region, making colour itself a branch of painting. Farinato carried that Verona school forward with bold colour and strong design.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pasto:
Pasto is a Colombian see, suffragan of Popayan, cut from it by Pius IX's bull of 10 April 1859. It lies in Cauca state, bounded north by Garzon and Popayan dioceses and south by Ecuador's Napo vicariate. Its bishop Adolfo Perea, born in 1853 in Popayan diocese and elected on 16 December 1907, followed Ezequiel Moreno, transferred to Pasto in 1893.

The diocese counts 315,640 Catholics, 41,000 pagan Indians, 68 parishes, 90 secular and 23 regular priests, and 133 churches or chapels. Pasto town, about 12,000 people, is well built and trades busily between Colombia and Ecuador, at the eastern foot of La Galera volcano, 8,650 feet up. Founded in 1539, taken by Bolivar in 1822, and shaken by an 1834 earthquake, it holds churches, a seminary, a Jesuit college, and a Sisters of Charity hospital.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-pistoia-and-p:
Pistoia and Prato form a diocese in the province of Florence. Pistoia sits beneath the Apennines in the Ombrone valley, its chief industries paper and straw goods. Its cathedral goes back to the fifth century, though fires harmed it repeatedly before the thirteenth, when Nicolò Pisano gave it its present shape. Its outer walls are inlaid with black and white marble bands.

Pistoia first appears in history with Catiline's conspiracy in 62 BC, becoming important only after the sixth century. Bishops ruled it first, then stewards serving Tuscany's Marquis, and it was the first town to establish independence after Countess Matilda's death. A Ghibelline town, it was compelled by Florence to become Guelph after Frederick II's death, and in 1351 Florence gained final mastery over it. Clement IX hailed from Pistoia.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-poggio-mirtet:
Poggio Mirteto, a diocese of central Italy in the province of Perugia, has its city on a fair hill beside the River Sole, amid rich land of herbs, grain, grapes, and pasture. Ruins of villas and aqueducts lie thick there, and Terentius Varro's villa stood close by.

For years the town obeyed the Abbot of Farfa, whose house now serves as the bishop's residence. Sabina gave up its territory in 1841, when the old collegiate church rose to cathedral rank and a seminary opened. Nicolò Crispigni served as first bishop. The diocese holds thirty-eight parishes and 32,600 souls.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-quito:
Quito, formerly San Francisco de Quito, capital of Ecuador, stands just south of the Equator and 114 miles inland from the Pacific. This encyclopedia entry sets it at about 9,300 feet, with some 70,000 people, mostly mestizos. It served as capital of the Incas Huaynacapac and Atahualpa, and Rumiñahui burnt it in 1533. Sebastián de Belalcázar captured it the next year. Charles the Fifth made it a city in 1541, and in 1565 it became the seat of a separate Franciscan province.

Quito belonged to Peru until 1718, when it passed to Nueva Granada. Its Jesuit seminary formed the centre of church studies for all middle and northern South America, while Dominicans and Augustinians ran high schools there. An earthquake ruined the city in 1735. Church histories, a study of the Quito press, and the diocesan bulletin supply its sources on an Andean capital of faith and learning.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ralph-de-dice:
Ralph de Diceto, Dean of Saint Paul's, London, and chronicler, bears a name that cannot be tied to any place in England. This encyclopedia entry suggests he may therefore have been born in France. His birth falls between 1120 and 1130, and he died on 22 November 1202. Twice a student at Paris, he gained the archdeaconry of Middlesex in 1152 and became dean of Saint Paul's in 1180. For fifty years he befriended bishops of London.

Among those friends stood Gilbert Foliot, leader of the royalist party among the bishops and adversary of Archbishop Saint Thomas. Friendship with Foliot and admiration for Henry the Second drew Ralph toward the royalists in the Becket controversy, but not wholly. He kept something of the wide outlook of the twelfth century, and he showed sympathy for his archbishop at the Council of Northampton. Bishop Stubbs's Rolls Series edition of 1876 remains the best edition of his works.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-recanati-and-:
The Diocese of Recanati and Loreto, in the province of Ancona in central Italy, takes its name from the people of ancient Recina, capital of Picenum. This encyclopedia entry tells that after Alaric devastated their country, those people founded Recanati. Claudius, present at the Council of Rimini, is thought to have been Bishop of Recina. Recanati answered to the Diocese of Umana until 1240, when Gregory the Ninth stripped Osimo of its see and moved it to Recanati.

Ranieri, Bishop of Osimo, became the first Bishop of Recanati. The see swung back and forth with politics. It was lost in 1263 when Recanati backed Manfred, restored in 1289, moved to Macerata in 1320, and joined with Macerata as a diocese again in 1357. Marino del Tocco, elected in 1412, faced a contested election from the party of John the Twenty-Third and King Ladislaus. The diocese counted 26,000 people, with 48 secular and 40 regular priests.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ruvo-and-bito:
Ruvo and Bitonto form a diocese in the province of Bari in southern Italy. Ruvo, the ancient Rubi, sits on a calcareous hill with a fine Norman cathedral of the eleventh century. Legend says St Peter preached here and appointed St Cletus, later pope, as first bishop. Joannes, mentioned in 493, is the first prelate known with certainty.

Other bishops include Arnolfo, first undoubted Bishop of Bitonto in 1087, Cornelio Musso, distinguished at Trent in 1544, and Fabrizio Carafa, founder of a literary academy in 1622. In 1818 Ruvo was united to Bitonto. Chief events are Gonsalvo di Cordova's capture of Ruvo in 1503, beating the French, and the 1734 battle of Bitonto, where Spaniards beat Austrians. The united dioceses hold 25,000 inhabitants, a Franciscan friary, and seven religious houses.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-saint-otto:
Otto of Bamberg, born about 1060 into a Swabian noble family, died on 30 June 1139. Priest, imperial chancellor under Henry IV, and bishop of Bamberg from 1102, he steered a middle course in the investiture struggle, the fight over who appointed bishops. His entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia presents a statesman-bishop who refused to become any party's tool.

He would not be consecrated by a schismatic bishop, declared loyalty to Rome, and received the pallium, the archbishop's woollen band, from Paschal II in 1111. Later he turned his energy to mission work among the Pomeranians, founding churches and winning converts in a pagan land. The entry balances his court career with his missionary journeys, showing why Bamberg honoured him as apostle and saint.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-salto:
Salto, a diocese in Uruguay suffragan of Montevideo, was erected with Melo by Leo XIII on 19 April 1897 at Montevideo's bishop's request and with the government's consent. Montevideo rose to an archdiocese, with two titular bishops named to help the new archbishop, but hostile politics left the new sees unfilled as late as December 1911. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia describes a diocese waiting for its bishop.

Covering the north-west of Uruguay, the departments of Río Negro, Paysandú, Salto, Artigas, and Tacuarembó, it spans 25,700 square miles with about 197,000 people. The town of Salto, 12,000 strong on the Río de la Plata opposite Concordia in Argentina, trades widely and links by boat and rail with Montevideo and Buenos Aires. Paysandú, with 16,000 people, is another busy commercial centre.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-san-miniato:
San Miniato, a city and diocese in Florence province in central Italy, first appears in the eighth century as Vicus Wallari, home to an oratory of Miniato, the martyr also called Mennas. From the eleventh century its people warred often with nearby San Genesio, where Tuscan nobles and cities met in council and treaty. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows an imperial town swallowed by Florence.

The town backed the emperors, hosted German soldiers, and won many imperial privileges. In 1248 San Genesio was razed, and its chapter moved to San Miniato, whose chapter head gained episcopal rank in 1526. Florence seized the town in 1397 and sought a bishopric for it in 1408, but only in 1622 did San Miniato become a diocese, with Francesco Nori as first bishop in 1624.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-casa-di:
The Holy House of Loreto, among Italy's most famous shrines since the fifteenth century, stands inside a great domed basilica. The small town of Loreto lies a few miles south of Ancona near the sea. The basilica, built and adorned over more than a century by many famous artists, serves merely as a setting for a tiny cottage within. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia examines a beloved legend with care.

Though its rough walls were raised and cased outside in sculptured marble, the cottage inside measures only thirty-one feet by thirteen. An altar stands beneath an age-blackened statue of the Virgin and Child, and the inscription, Here the Word was made flesh, marks it as the Nazareth home of the Holy Family. The entry weighs the tradition of its miraculous move against the historical record.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-santa-maria-d:
Santa Maria de Monserrato, an abbey nullius in Brazil, stands at the centre of a Benedictine restoration entrusted to the Beuron congregation on 24 April 1895 under Dom Gerard van Caloen. The Rio de Janeiro abbey itself, founded in 1589, became an abbey nullius by decree of 15 August 1907. Its entry in the 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia follows monks into the Amazon borderland.

The same decree detached the Rio Branco district from the diocese of Amazones and placed it under the abbot. Bounded by Venezuela, British Guiana, and the Branco and Negro rivers, the mission land held 6,000 Catholic Brazilians and 50,000 pagan Indians. Holy Ghost Fathers Libermann and Berthon had visited it briefly in early 1898, working among Catholics scattered along the Branco's banks.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-sorrento:
Sorrento was an archdiocese on the southern arm of the Gulf of Naples, and this entry blends its church history with its ancient past. Sheltered by Mount Sant' Angelo and perched high above the sea, the city drew summer visitors even then. While its peninsula, dotted with Roman villas, stretched between the gulfs of Naples and Amalfi.

Tradition credits Ulysses as founder, and the entry notes temples of Ceres, Venus. And Minerva, coins of its own, alliance with Rome in 312 before Christ, capture by Hannibal, and a colony planted by Augustus. From Byzantine rule onward it kept its own rulers, and the archdiocese, with Castellamare as suffragan, carried that long civic story into modern church life.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spirito-santo:
Spirito Santo, or Espirito Santo, was a Brazilian diocese, suffragan to Rio de Janeiro and established in 1896, covering the whole state of Espirito Santo. This entry gives its shape in 1911: twenty-eight municipalities, 202,000 Catholics, twenty secular priests, and fifteen friars, governed from Victoria, the state capital and bishop's seat.

Catholic schooling in Victoria included a college of secondary instruction run by secular priests with federal privileges, and a girls' college under the Sisters of Charity. The same sisters nursed in the Hospital da Misericordia, beside the Santa Casa de Misericordia, a charity founded in 1545 and granted Lisbon's privileges in 1606. Together they give a compact record of church and charity on Brazil's coast.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-spoleto:
Spoleto was an Umbrian archdiocese whose city, perched on a spur of Monteluco in the Sibylline Mountains, had been a fortress in every age. This entry describes a place of marble quarries, coal mines. And truffle woods, and a cathedral begun in 617 by Duke Theudelapius, with a tenth-century campanile, a 1207 facade mosaic. And an interior restored by Bernini holding frescoes by Pinturicchio and Fra Filippo Lippi, buried there.

Beyond the Porta della Torre stands the fifth-century church of San Pietro with twelfth-century sculpture, and the entry moves from monuments to diocesan history, bishops, and institutions. Readers get both an art lover's Spoleto and a church historian's, in a city where the steep rock shaped sacred and military life alike.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-alto:
St. Alto was a recluse and missionary in Bavaria about 750, and this entry pieces together a life known only in broad strokes. Described variously as Anglo-Saxon and Irish, he bore the undoubtedly Irish name Alt, lived for a time as a hermit clearing wild forest land. And then founded a Benedictine monastery on the spot, now Altomunster in the diocese of Freising, on land granted by King Pepin.

St. Boniface is said to have come to dedicate the church about 750, and a charter survives bearing the signature Alto reclausus, probably from his hermit days. His year of death is unknown, though he is commemorated on 9 February, and the entry follows Altomunster through Hun raids and noble plunder to restoration about the year 1000.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-melito:
Melito, bishop of Sardis in the second century, survives chiefly through the lists and fragments preserved by Eusebius. Little is known of his life, though a letter of Polycrates calls him a great authority of the Asian Church who held the Quartodeciman dating of Easter. Hippolytus counts him among writers who taught two natures in Christ, and Jerome reports that many faithful esteemed him a prophet.

Almost all his numerous works have perished, but Eusebius kept their titles and some extracts. Chief among them stands an Apology to Marcus Aurelius, urging the emperor to examine charges against Christians and end persecution. A separate Syriac apology, once tied to his name, looks Syrian in origin. The entry gathers what can still be known of a lost voice of early Asia Minor.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-stephan-szant:
Stephan Szanto, a Hungarian Jesuit, laboured to plant Catholic missions and a Hungarian college in Rome. Born in the diocese of Raab in 1541, he finished studies at Vienna, joined that diocese, and in 1560 was sent to the German College at Rome. There he joined the Jesuits and was ordained priest after his novitiate.

In 1566 he returned to Vienna and taught at Nagy-Szombat, then lectured on philosophy at Vienna and Graz. In 1568 he worked to plant a Catholic mission in Transylvania, where Protestantism advanced rapidly, a project he pursued in Rome after being summoned there in 1579 as Hungarian penitentiary. His plan for a Hungarian college on the German College's model won Gregory XIII's approval and opened on 28 May 1579, but the pope soon merged it with the German College. Szanto left Rome late in 1579 for Transylvania. He died at Olmütz in 1612.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-taranto:
Taranto is a diocese of southern Italy on a bay of its gulf. The old city stood on an island joined by two bridges to the mainland, where the new city stands. Islets guard the great commercial harbour, and the old city forms a smaller military port second only to Spezzia. Strong forts guard coast and islets, export trade is large, and warship building thrives. Fishing flourishes in the small harbour.

Its eleventh-century cathedral, partly rebuilt, holds a silver statue of St Cathaldus. Its marble chapel carries a fresco by Paolo de Matteis. Taras, founded by Spartans in 707 BC, grew from aristocratic republic to democracy. It hired foreign captains including Pyrrhus and fell to Rome in 272 after Beneventum. The archdiocese now counts 26 parishes, 261 priests, and 220,300 people, with Castellaneta and Oria as suffragans.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-the-royal-vet:
Crown control over Catholic bishops in Ireland and England, known as the Royal Veto, is the controversy examined here. Toward the close of the eighteenth century penal laws still stood on the books, though less strictly enforced. Catholics formed Ireland's vast majority, their sympathies suspected toward France, and penal laws had failed their purpose, so government sought other means.

Bishops and priests swayed the people powerfully, and ministers hoped that directing episcopal influence would secure allegiance and fetter the Church. Maynooth College's founding offered an opening: would bishops accept state appointment of its president and professors? Negotiations, refusals, and the veto's long shadow fill a revealing chapter of church-state struggle.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-toronto:
Toronto is an archdiocese in Ontario, Canada, first covering all of Upper Canada west of Newcastle district, later limited to York, Simcoe, Ontario, Peel, Dufferin, Lincoln and Welland counties. Its first missionary was the Recollect Joseph Le Caron, who said Mass on Georgian Bay in 1615, opening the Huron missions whose heroism the entry recalls.

After the Huron nations fell, few priests worked the region until the nineteenth century, when Macdonell and others served York and Niagara. Kingston diocese split on 17 December 1841 to form Toronto under Bishop Power. Later archbishops include Lynch, who brought new religious orders to the diocese and saw it raised to metropolitan rank in 1870, Walsh, who died in 1898 after founding St. John's Industrial School, O'Connor, who became archbishop in 1899 and resigned in 1908, and his successor McEvay.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-trivento:
A diocese in southern Italy, suffragan of Beneventum, whose earliest bishop was St. Castus, of uncertain date, whom local legend places in the fourth century. Later bishops include Leo, a monk intruded and deposed by Agapetus II in 946, and the Franciscan Luca, exiled by King Manfred in 1226.

Pietro dell' Aquila, bishop in 1348, was noted for learning, and the Moriconda bishops of 1582 and 1717 both restored the cathedral, the later one also rebuilding the episcopal residence. The diocese counts 58 parishes with 130,000 souls, 160 secular priests and three religious houses, a compact southern see with a long episcopal roll.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ugento:
Ugento is a small harbour city in Apulia, on the Gulf of Tarentum, known in ancient times as Uxentum. It claims a founder named Uxens, mentioned in Virgil's Aeneid. In antiquity it ranked as an important town before Turkish raiders destroyed it in 1537. Under Byzantine rule it had Greek bishops, and its Latin bishops begin with the Benedictine Simeon, of unknown date. Later figures include St Charles Borromeo and the poet Minturno.

The entry follows the diocese through the Council of Trent, where its bishop Desiderio Mazzapica won distinction, and through the great canonist Agostino Barbosa in the seventeenth century. In 1818 the suppressed diocese of Alessano was joined to Ugento. The Greek rite, once flourishing in the region, was abolished by Bishop Ercole in 1591. A short civic and church history, it suits readers tracing Apulia's layered Greek, Roman, and Latin past.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-william-peyto:
William Peyto was a Franciscan cardinal who defied Henry VIII over his divorce and paid with exile. His parentage was long unknown, but he was son of Edward Peyto of Chesterton and Goditha Throckmorton. Schooled by Grey Friars, he took degrees at Oxford and Cambridge, became a Queen's fellow in 1506 and a Franciscan famed for holiness, then confessor to Princess Mary and provincial of England. In 1532 he denounced Henry's divorce to the king's face.

Imprisoned until year's end, Peyto fled abroad, working for Catholic interests at Antwerp, and in 1539 Henry attainted him with Pole's circle while he sheltered in Italy. Paul III named him Bishop of Salisbury in March 1543, but he never held the see, resigning it under Mary and retiring to Greenwich. Paul IV made him cardinal in June 1557, though Mary barred the hat, and he died in 1558 or 1559, tradition saying a London mob stoned him.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-zucchetto:
Zucchetto is the small, round skullcap of the ecclesiastic, from zucca, head. Its official name is pileolus; other names are berettino, calotte, subbiretum because worn under the biretta, submitrale because worn under the mitre, and soli-deo. The pope's zucchetto is white and the cardinals' red, even when the cardinal belongs to an order. Cardinals who had been secular priests received the red zucchetto and red biretta in 1464 from Paul II; cardinals from the regulars gained both in 1591.

Bishops wear violet, and other ecclesiastics, including prelates unless granted a special privilege, wear black. It cannot be said positively when the zucchetto became customary, probably not before the thirteenth century. It appears on cardinals in the fresco Saint Francis before Honorius III, painted about 1290 at Assisi, and under the tiara in Clement VI's tomb effigy.
christianity-its-evidences-its-origin-it:
Annie Besant wrote Part II of The Freethinker's Text-Book as a case for rejecting Christianity outright. Her first section attacks the evidences. Marvels fill the Gospel story — a guiding star, massacres, healings, a three-hour darkness, an empty tomb. Yet contemporary history, she argues, shows no ripple from any of it. Josephus, a painstaking historian of that very age, is her chief witness.

Lost gospels are then catalogued by the dozen. Gospels of Judas, Thomas, Peter, Eve, and the Egyptians appear in her list. The notes of time for Christ's birth in Matthew and Luke are called irreconcilable. Strauss's Life of Jesus supplies long quotations. Origin, morality, and history are promised the same treatment in later sections.
crito:
Plato set his dialogue Crito in an Athens prison cell in the last days of Socrates, and Benjamin Jowett translated this edition. Crito, an old friend, arrives before dawn with money, helpers, and a plan to smuggle Socrates out. Athens has condemned the philosopher to die, and escape would be easy. Socrates refuses to move until the argument is settled.

Question by question, Socrates shows that running away would break his lifelong agreement with the laws of Athens. Near the end the laws themselves speak, asking what gratitude a citizen owes the city that raised him. Crito leaves persuaded, or at least silenced. Few short works carry this much weight about duty, justice, and civil obedience.
doe-osti-17084195-velocity-resolved-kine:
Christopher Kliewer, Shinae Kim, Eric Smoll, and Judit Zador of Sandia describe a new microscope for gas surface chemistry in report SAND2026-26917R, printed September 2026. Reaction rates at catalyst surfaces are hard to pin down, because products leave the surface at varied angles and speeds. Their instrument images ions by velocity to read those details.

Electrode stacks pull ions from a catalyst sample through a pinhole in a velocity mapped plane, filtering by sideways speed before they strike a position detector about 1,250 millimeters away. Simulations in the report map flight time against mass, image blur against pinhole size and gas temperature, and trajectories for ions born off center. The design work supports later rate measurements.
doe-osti-17084218-post-optimality-analys:
Joseph Hart, Bart van Bloemen Waanders, Madhusudan Madhavan, and Mauro Perego of Sandia address a trust problem in optimization in report SAND2026-26688, printed September 2026. Decisions often come from optimizing a cheap, low fidelity model, because the accurate model is too slow to run many times. The question is how the best answer shifts when the model itself is off.

Their framework, HDSA-MD, fuses a small number of high fidelity runs into the cheap optimization and updates the answer after the fact. Uncertainty is carried through, so trust in the decision matches how much accurate data exists. Chapters summarize five journal articles behind the method, a real time optimization demonstration, and the software built to run it.
doe-osti-2586879-expanding-activity-allo:
Alanie Keith, a summer 2025 research intern at Oak Ridge National Laboratory, wrote this study with Joseph Tuccillo of the lab's Geospatial Science and Human Security Division. It looks at exercise access in Clarksville, Tennessee. The work expands UrbanPop, a framework that builds synthetic populations and allocates their daily activities. Here the agents are sent to fitness centers across the Clarksville metro area.

The study reads access through geography, demographics, and time of week. Senior and retired agents consistently travel longer distances to exercise. The authors link that pattern to their tendency to live farther from the metro center. Every demographic group travels farther on weekends than on weekdays. Weekday distance seems to bite harder, the authors argue, because work and school compete for time. The work shows how simulated populations can surface equity questions about everyday services.
doe-osti-2588878-photovoltaic-systems-ev:
Charles Robinson of Sandia National Laboratories presented this program overview, SAND2025-11456R, in Davos, Switzerland, in fall 2025. It profiles the Photovoltaic Systems Evaluation Laboratory. The laboratory is funded by the Department of Energy's Solar Energy Technologies Office. It is the nation's test bench for solar hardware. If a panel, cell, or system claims performance, PSEL can measure whether it delivers.

Core capabilities include the PV Proving Grounds, with solar cell, module, and full system testing, a weather station, and long term evaluation sites. Regional Test Centers extend the work across climates. Other programs cover tracker optimization and testing of parts such as encapsulants, backsheets, and connectors. The PV Accelerator for Cell Technologies, led by Josh Stein, serves as a neutral judge for new perovskite and organic minimodules. Modeling tools and radiometer calibration round out the portfolio.
doe-osti-2999826-using-stable-isotopes-i:
Joseph Galewsky of the University of New Mexico wrote this final report for award SC0023350 on reading the sky through water itself. Water vapour carries stable isotopes, heavier and lighter versions of hydrogen and oxygen, in ratios that shift as air mixes, rises and rains out. Those ratios can trace how clouds, aerosols and rain interact, a tangle that climate models struggle to pin down.

Two field studies anchor the work. In TRACER-iso, during a 2022 Houston-area campaign, a laser isotope analyser watched sea breezes push inland at La Porte, Texas. The team logged 46 sea breeze events and found the cool marine air kept a distinct isotope signature as it mixed with continental air. In EPCAPE, at Scripps Pier in La Jolla, information-theory tools sorted which factors, mixing depth, stability, source region, truly control the vapour's make-up. An isotope-tracking model rounds out the project.
doe-osti-3003128-the-green-omics-of-nutr:
Bruce Hungate of Northern Arizona University leads a four-institution team in the final report for DOE award DE-SC0020172, submitted September 11, 2025. The project ran from September 2019 to September 2024. Its question: how do soil microbes control nutrient cycling as soils warm? The team used isotope-enabled 'omics methods, reading genes, proteins, and growth in soil communities.

The framework, called GREEN 'omics, ties microbial growth rate, growth efficiency, and nutrient stoichiometry together. Partners at West Virginia University, Lawrence Livermore, and Pacific Northwest contributed. The report recommends folding the trait-based data into Earth system models to sharpen climate projections. It also flags soil viruses, including highly active phages the team found, as a next frontier. All data and code were archived publicly under the project's data plan.
doe-osti-3005572-using-molecular-dynamic:
Bastien Henri Farnault tests a shortcut in Los Alamos report LA-UR-25-31376, issued November 18, 2025. The problem is melting curves: the line on a pressure-temperature map where a solid turns liquid. Measuring that line in simulation usually takes heavy computation. A newer approach claims to read it from simpler quantities, and this project checks the claim with molecular dynamics.

Three model materials carry the test: Lennard-Jones, Yukawa, and hard-sphere potentials. The analysis leans on logarithmic derivative curves and the self-diffusion coefficient, computed both from particle displacements and from velocity correlations. Free-volume pictures for the hard-sphere case appear in an appendix, with packing fractions tabulated from 0.36 to 0.55. Reports like this validate methods before they are trusted on real materials at extreme conditions.
doe-osti-3011609-support-of-the-us-japan:
United States and Japanese photosynthesis researchers met at Arizona State University for a three day workshop recorded in the final report for award DE-SC0024720. Kevin Redding organised the November 6 to 8, 2023 meeting in the Old Main ballroom on the Tempe campus. Graham Peers and Chihiro Azai co organised. The workshop aimed to deepen collaboration on energy transduction in photosynthetic organisms across the two communities.

Thirteen invited speakers came from each country. Support favoured younger scientists: United States graduate students and postdocs had registration covered in full, with partial travel help for those from outside Arizona with need. The small format let students meet senior researchers whose papers they read.
doe-osti-3012753-mitigation-for-the-demo:
Gregory M. Haynes of the Desert Research Institute wrote this cultural resources mitigation report, submitted August 2025, for the demolition of dormitory buildings 12-32, 12-34, 12-35, and 12-37 at the Nevada National Security Site. The four buildings belong to the Area 12 Camp Historic District in Nye County, Nevada. Federal preservation law calls for recording historic buildings before they are removed.

The dormitories were the first permanent housing built in Area 12 and housed workers supporting underground nuclear testing from 1986 to 1992, the final Cold War years. They count as contributing elements of the district for both their support role and their distinctive motel-style design. The mitigation updates their Architectural Resource Assessment forms with current-condition photographs, plans, and sketches, preserving the record even as the buildings come down.
doe-osti-3013879-computerized-assignment:
Norman Boyd and Hy Tran wrote Sandia report SAND2025-15458, printed December 2025, on computerizing reviewer assignment for the Truman Fellowship. Fellowship programs must match each applicant with qualified reviewers while balancing workloads and avoiding lopsided assignments. Done by hand, the matching is slow and hard to keep fair as applicant pools grow.

The authors define requirements, then formulate the matching as an integer optimization problem solved with the PuLP library in Python. Workload rules guarantee each reviewer a bounded share: total assignments scale as twice the applicant count divided by the reviewer count, split between primary and secondary roles. Example inputs and outputs show the workflow. The report closes with sibling applications, including mentor-mentee pairing, large project task assignment, and shift scheduling.
doe-osti-3014129-human-factors-and-techn:
Clemson University's final scientific report, by Yunyi Jia, Johnell Brooks, Haotian Su, and co-authors, studies why riders resist pooling rideshares and how design can change that. Pooled rideshare packs strangers into one vehicle, saving energy per trip, but most users still ride solo. The team treated acceptance as a human factors problem, not just a pricing one.

National surveys in several phases, including a dataset spanning New York, San Francisco, Detroit, Chicago, Atlanta, and Austin, fed behavioral choice models. Workshops distilled the findings into 95 actionable design items across nine categories, from driver and passenger selection to accessibility. A simulation platform and improved pooling algorithms completed the pipeline. The conclusion: fixing human factors barriers is essential before pooled rideshare delivers its energy savings.
doe-osti-3014902-exploring-actinide-nano:
Actinide nanocrystal growth is the subject of a Washington State University final report under award DE-SC0025546, led by Liane Moreau. When actinide oxides shrink to nanometer size, most atoms sit at the surface and electronic behavior shifts, yet growth rules for elements from thorium to americium remain poorly mapped.

Year one focused on uranium and thorium while students trained for transuranium work. Removing the solvent and raising amine concentration lengthened thorium oxide nanorods toward nanowires, one of several synthesis trends the team tracked with advanced X-ray tools. Two manuscripts are in preparation, on thorium oxide growth mechanisms and on a glovebox heating block system for microscale synthesis. The project then closed at Washington State as the investigator moved to the University of Wyoming.
doe-osti-3015274-benefits-of-energy-stor:
Energy storage benefits for Washington, D.C. are priced in PNNL-38942, a Pacific Northwest National Laboratory analysis dated January 2026 for the District's Department of Energy and Environment. Storage earns its keep in a dense city grid by shaving peaks, deferring wires upgrades, and cutting losses. Jeremy Twitchell led the author team.

The transmission and distribution numbers are concrete. In the PEPCO zone, enough storage to shave 1 percent of peak load saves about 1.8 million dollars a year; at a 15 percent peak reduction, avoided transmission deferrals reach almost 28 million dollars annually. For the D.C. subzone alone, savings run from 0.6 to 8.9 million dollars. Avoided distribution losses are far smaller, from 740 to 11,000 dollars in the PEPCO zone, and the study notes that distribution capital deferral value still needs project-specific data.
doe-osti-3018739-scaling-spectroradiomet:
Thomas A Reichardt, Christopher Katinas, and Jerilyn A Timlin of Sandia wrote this January 2026 report, SAND2026-16518R, on watching algae ponds by light. The work sat inside DISCOVR, a BETO-funded project on screening and cultivar optimization for algae biofuels. Ponds at the Arizona Center for Algae Technology and Innovation grew varied strains under the sensors. Spectroradiometric monitoring reads reflected spectra to predict biomass concentration at high frequency. It also aims to flag pond crashes early, from pest signals or shifts in the algal host.

The report's assigned deliverable is deployment advice at factory-farm scale. Laboratory hyperspectral scenes ran 275 by 290 pixels across 51 wavelengths, at 250-millisecond integrations. Automated analysis was tuned to feed pond automation decisions. For growers, the promise is a pond that reports its own health hourly instead of by manual sampling. This summary carries the method from bench scenes to production ponds.
doe-osti-3024595-hanford-site-post-fire-:
M L Johnson and N J Exe of Hanford Mission Integration Solutions tracked how vegetation came back after fire at the Hanford Site through calendar year 2025. Their report is HNF-72995, Revision 0, published March 2026. Burned shrub-steppe can recover as native grassland or tip toward invasive weeds, and the difference decides habitat quality for decades. Crews revisited monitoring transects and compared native and non-native cover over time.

The pattern was consistent across most areas. Non-native vegetation surged after the fire and passed native cover at most transects, while in one badly hit area almost no native vegetation has recovered and natives were nearly eliminated. Lately the trend has bent: non-native cover has fallen over the last two years. It peaked back in 2023 by the authors' account, and now approaches a lower equilibrium as succession settles.
doe-osti-3362748-gas-gap-calorimeter-siz:
Ilyas Yilgor, Jeremy L. Hartvigsen, Zachary D. Sellers, and Piyush Sabharwall of Idaho National Laboratory, with Katrina M. Sweetland of Los Alamos, deliver design tools in report INL/RPT-25-86034, dated June 2025. Gas-gap calorimeters measure the heat pouring off a heat pipe, a sealed tube that moves heat for microreactor tests. Getting the size right matters: too weak a cooler ruins the test conditions, and sloppy sizing ruins the heat reading itself.

Two tools, one in Excel and one in MATLAB, handle both sizing a new unit and rating an existing one. Their study sweeps argon share in the gas gap from none to full, input power from 500 to 5,000 watts, and four gap widths from 0.042 to 0.090 inches. Surface glow factors, called emissivities, were varied too, since they drift with heat.
doe-osti-3367451-project-2-8-biological-:
Georgetown University final technical report, dated June 3, 2026 and led by Christopher Loffredo, closes Project 2.8, the specimen repository supporting the Mayak Project's studies of Russian nuclear workers. The Southern Urals Biophysics Institute holds tissues and blood from workers at the Mayak plutonium facility, a unique resource for radiation health research. This report hands the repository fully to the Russian institute.

Georgetown's team steps back to voluntary advice: the institute assumes freezer costs, specimen requests, and the repository website. Specimens held at Georgetown cannot yet be returned; no shipper currently delivers them to Russia, so they remain in shared-resource storage. Advice includes round-the-clock freezer alarms and periodic specimen quality checks. The document is a transition plan, candid about geopolitics blocking science logistics.
doe-osti-3376159-community-resilience-th:
A final technical report for Department of Energy award DE-EE0010425 closes a GE Vernova Advanced Research project on faster power restoration after outages. Xian Guo served as principal investigator. The project ran from August 2023 to April 2024. Its wager is that homes and small sites now hold real power assets: solar, batteries, and flexible loads. Add cheap sensors to that mix, and a utility can map damage fast and switch power back in a smart order.

The team wrote software specs for the core algorithms. One finds the true edge of an outage from live voltage reads. A second hunts for usable distributed resources in the dark zone. A third picks a feasible path to bring them online. Test cases were built on a GridLab-D software-in-the-loop rig. The frame aims at fair recovery too, not just fast recovery, so no district is left last by habit.
doe-osti-3377891-sam-battery-modeling-fo:
Brian Mirletz of the National Laboratory of the Rockies walks the APPA Energy Storage Working Group through battery modeling in the System Advisor Model. The slides are dated March 24, 2026. SAM is free software, developed at the laboratory with Department of Energy funding. It pairs performance modeling with financial analysis for renewable energy and storage projects.

The model structure runs from weather data and system specs to hourly or sub-hourly production. From there it flows to cash flow, net present value, levelized cost of energy, and payback period. The battery sections stress lifetime modeling. A cycle and calendar model uses a Rainflow stress algorithm. Chemistry-specific analytical models cover nickel manganese cobalt on graphite. They also cover lithium manganese oxide on lithium titanate.
doe-osti-3385039-on-transforming-the-spe:
A Sandia National Laboratories memorandum, SAND2026-23421R, dated June 2026, by Tucker Haydon, Eryn Jaramillo, and Brandon Simmons, derives the transform of the specific force vector. The setting is an Earth-centered, Earth-fixed inertial navigation system. An inertial measurement unit accumulates the specific force on the sensor over small time windows. That accumulation happens in the sensor's own frame. But the force must be integrated in the navigation frame, and the two frames rotate against each other.

A correction is therefore needed. It accounts both for the frame difference and for how that difference changes over time. Many references give the derivation in abbreviated form, with assumptions left unstated. The memo's stated purpose is to close that gap. It gives the full derivation with every assumption spelled out. The work is specific to the ECEF frame but written clearly enough to adapt.
expositions-of-holy-scripture-second-kin:
Maclaren's Expositions volume on Second Kings and later histories spans many Old Testament books. Alexander Maclaren begins at Second Kings chapter VIII and runs to that book's end. Chronicles, Ezra, and Nehemiah follow. Esther, Job, Proverbs, and Ecclesiastes complete the volume.

Second Kings entries include The Story of Hazael and Impure Zeal. Hezekiah, A Pattern of Devout Life uses chapters XVIII and XIX. The Rediscovered Law and Its Effects treats chapter XXII. Chronicles gives David's Choristers and David's Charge to Solomon. The Duty of Every Day comes from Second Chronicles VIII. Maclaren finds a sermon text in narrative corners others pass by. The volume shows his range across the history books.
florenz-quellen-shinto:
Karl Florenz published his Shinto sourcebook in German in 1919. The Historical Sources of the Shinto Religion was the first of its kind. Florenz ranked as the finest German Japanologist of his generation.

The Kojiki and the Nihongi supply the book's core ancient texts. Old Norito prayers join them in careful, scholarly German dress. Florenz guides readers through myth, rite, and imperial cult with notes. Students gained a firm path into Japan's native faith from his work. The sourcebook still anchors study of Shinto's oldest written records in the West. Florenz's care with hard texts set a standard for those who followed.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-PassporttoAssas:
An advertisement promotes 'Passport to Assassination,' a book about Lee Harvey Oswald. Its author is Oleg Maximovich Nechiporenko, a retired colonel of the KGB. The book was translated from the Russian. Nechiporenko had dealt with Oswald in Mexico City, where Oswald visited the Soviet consulate weeks before the assassination.

A KGB officer's memoir of Oswald was a publishing event of the post-Cold War years. The Soviet file on Oswald had been one of the case's locked rooms. The advertisement sells that access: the other side's officer, telling the story in English. It preserves the pitch made to Western readers, and the credential it rested on.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-WheelerBurtonKS: PM, the New York daily, reported a meeting between Senators Burton Wheeler and Gerald Nye and a man named Kamp. Wheeler and Nye were leading isolationists before the Second World War, opposed to American entry into the conflict. Their meetings drew press attention because both men shaped the foreign policy fight of their day. The short article preserves one such encounter as the paper reported it.
govdocs-archive_org-the-great-ufo-hoax-t: Gregory M. Kanon argues the opposite of most UFO books: the whole phenomenon is a deliberate hoax. His 1997 book, The Great UFO Hoax, promises a final solution to the UFO mystery. Kanon treats sightings, stories, and famous cases as parts of a made-up system that serves its makers. Skeptical readers get a full case here, built to explain not just a few sightings but the entire belief.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_foia_FOI:
The world's first freedom of information act dates to 1766, two and a half centuries before this briefing book marked the anniversary in December 2016. Lauren Harper edited the set, number 568. Its hero is Finland's Anders Chydenius, an early champion of open records.

By 2016, freedom of information laws had spread to 113 countries. The posting argues that the United States law still has room to grow if America wants to lead on transparency. The long view is the point: a practice now treated as normal began as a radical idea in eighteenth-century Finland and Sweden.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_mexico_U:
Since 2007 the United States has run its Mexico policy through a small circle of Mexican partner officials, under the Mérida Initiative. This briefing book, posted in December 2020, examines what happened when American prosecutions turned toward that circle. Corruption inside the partnership came into focus.

A wide-ranging aid program built on trusted counterparts faces an obvious risk: what if the counterparts are compromised? Court cases in the United States forced that question into the open. The documents here let readers trace how Washington's chosen partners were vetted, used, and in some cases prosecuted by the same government that had relied on them.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_russia-p:
Anatoly Chernyaev kept a diary while working inside the Soviet leadership, years before he became Mikhail Gorbachev's close aide. In May 2022, the National Security Archive published his diary for 1982 in English for the first time. The date marked what would have been his 101st birthday, and the edition was prepared by Svetlana Savranskaya.

The year 1982 sits in the run-up to perestroika, when Leonid Brezhnev was dying and reform had not yet begun. A diary like this records what a well-placed insider saw, heard, and worried about day by day, rather than what officials later claimed. For readers, it is a ground-level view of a tired system in its last years before change arrived.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_southern: Barack Obama's administration made declassification a tool of diplomacy with Argentina, promising to open American files on the dirty war of 1976 to 1983. A National Security Archive briefing book page carries that policy under the headline of Obama bringing declassified diplomacy to Argentina. The evidence preserved for this entry is the page capture alone, without the release's underlying documents, so it marks the moment and the policy rather than reproducing the records. Its companion postings in the Archive detail the examples of material such an opening could surface.

A court in Rome spent three years trying the cross-border repression that Latin America's military regimes ran together as Operation Condor. Briefing Book number 577, edited by Carlos Osorio and published in January 2017, covers the verdict: life sentences, summed up in the Archive's headline as condemned to life.

The National Security Archive supplied declassified evidence to the tribunal and welcomed the ruling as historic. That role matters here: secret American files, pried loose over years, ended up as proof in an Italian courtroom judging crimes committed in South America decades earlier. For readers, the posting shows the long road evidence travels, from classified vaults to a judge's bench, before justice of any kind becomes possible.
hamlet-the-first-bad-quarto:
Scholars call the first quarto of Hamlet, printed in 1603, the bad quarto, because its text is short, rough, and plainly reported from memory rather than set from the author's papers. This transcription keeps the original line breaks, notes the page breaks in the margin, and corrects no printing errors. The long s has been modernized, but no other spelling has been changed, the transcriber says. A note warns that an improved edition of the play exists elsewhere in the same library.

Whole speeches differ from the Hamlet everyone knows, and famous lines come out garbled or compressed. The interest is exactly there: this is the play as an actor's memory carried it, a rough draft of a masterpiece in motion. Students of Shakespeare use the bad quarto to study how plays were stolen, printed, and remade in his own lifetime.
history-of-liberia-johns-hopkins-univers:
J H T McPherson wrote this history of Liberia for the Johns Hopkins studies series, in 1891. It is a shortened form of his doctoral dissertation. McPherson calls it scarcely more than a brief sketch. Herbert B Adams edited the series in which it appeared.

Chapters trace the colonization idea and the movement behind it. Maryland's own colony in Liberia gets a full chapter. The republic's founding follows, with wars such as the Sinou river rising of 1857. McPherson weighs colonization as a check on the slave trade and a refuge for Black Americans. Scholars get a cool, early academic account.
introduction-to-the-philosophy-and-writi:
Thomas Taylor introduced the philosophy and writings of Plato in this study. He opens with Hierocles, that philosophy is the purification and perfection of human life. Plato is called its primary leader and hierophant. Taylor pictures philosophy as a luminous pyramid ending in Deity, based on the rational soul.

The soul on earth is in a fallen state, Taylor argues from Plato. It is an apostate from deity and an exile from light, in his reading. Ascents and descents through endless time fill his account of the soul's periods. The book is a Neoplatonic reading, fervent in tone.
itivuttaka-sujato:
Bhikkhu Sujato translated the Itivuttaka, meaning As It Was Said, into modern English. The collection holds 112 short sayings of the Buddha in the Khuddaka Nikaya. Each saying opens with the formula that names the book.

Teachings on greed, kindness, and heedfulness appear in compact prose and verse. Many sayings pair a prose statement with a verse restatement for memory. Tradition says a laywoman named Khujjuttara preserved these teachings by hearing them. Sujato's plain modern English, released freely, suits the terse originals. The Itivuttaka works as Buddhism's pocket wisdom for daily reflection. Its brevity hides a complete ethical teaching in miniature form here.
khuddakapatha-sujato:
Bhikkhu Sujato translated the Khuddakapatha, the Minor Readings, into modern English. The little book gathers nine short texts from the Khuddaka Nikaya. Novice monks across the Theravada world still learn it by heart.

Refuges, precepts, and blessings make up the beginner's prayer book of Buddhism. The famous Discourse on Goodwill, the Metta Sutta, stands among its nine pieces. Other texts praise the Buddha's virtues and answer a god's questions. Sujato's translation gives the whole set in clear English. Small in size, the Khuddakapatha stays central to daily Buddhist life. Two thousand years of beginners have started exactly here with these readings.
life-of-tecumseh-and-of-his-brother-the-:
Benjamin Drake published this life of Tecumseh in Cincinnati in 1841. E. Morgan and Company printed the volume there. Drake also wrote a life of Black Hawk and Queen City tales. A historical sketch of the Shawanoe Indians accompanies the biography.

Contents name Black-Hoof, Cornstalk, and Captain Logan first. Tecumseh's brothers include Tenskwatawa, called the Prophet. Early chapters cover Piqua's destruction and Tecumseh's first battle. He already worked to abolish the burning of prisoners, Drake reports. Cheeseekan, Sauweeseekau, and Nehasseemo appear among the brothers listed. Cherokee visits and southern battles interrupt Tecumseh's Ohio years.
lippincott-s-magazine-of-popular-literat:
The October 1877 Lippincott's, Volume Twenty, Number 118, opens in Chester. Two papers on Chester and the Dee lead the issue. Chester surrendered last to William the Conqueror, the article notes. It also fell last among cities for the Stuart king's cause.

Rome's Twentieth Legion once held Chester as a northwestern key. Coalfields, mills, and Liverpool's quays crowd its modern borders. Yet the city stays unique in architecture and position. Americans, the writer says, find it a lodestone for visits. Liverpool's quays and Manchester's grimy mills crowd Chester's borders. Architectural peculiarities make the old city a lodestone to Americans.
majjhima-nikaya-sujato:
Bhikkhu Sujato translated the Majjhima Nikaya, the Middle Discourses of the Buddha, into modern English. The collection holds 152 discourses of medium length from the Pali canon. It forms the second great collection of the Sutta Pitaka.

Many discourses stage conversations with kings, monks, wanderers, and skeptics. Teachings cover meditation, ethics, karma, and the nature of the self. Famous pieces include instructions on mindfulness and the simile of the raft. Sujato's plain English, released freely through SuttaCentral, favors clarity over ornament. The Majjhima is often called the heart of early Buddhism. New readers of the Buddha usually begin somewhere inside this collection.
marx-communist-manifesto:
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels published The Communist Manifesto in London in February 1848, weeks before revolutions swept Europe. The pamphlet was the program of the Communist League, a small band of exiled workers and thinkers. It runs barely thirty pages, and it changed the world.

The text tells history as a long fight between classes, now between owners and workers. It praises the energy of modern industry, then predicts its owners will dig its grave. Ten demands close the argument, from free schooling to steep income taxes. The call for workers of all lands to unite rings from its last page.
memoirs-of-general-lafayette-with-an-acc:
Samuel L. Knapp wrote memoirs of General Lafayette and his visit to America. The visit ran from August 15 to October 19, 1824. Rights were entered in Massachusetts on November 2, 1824, by E. G. House.

The editor admits the book was prepared in haste for the public. Yet he says that plea, in this case, is fully true. The tale ends with the celebration at Yorktown that October. A young nation's thanks to an old ally fills the account of his welcome. His landing on August 15 starts the count of days. Each port and town on the route adds its own welcome scene.
mother-stories-from-the-new-testament-a-:
The Henry Altemus Company of Philadelphia published this Bible storybook for mothers to read aloud. Its subtitle promises the best stories from the New Testament that mothers can tell their children. Forty-five illustrations accompany the retellings. The frontispiece shows little ones being brought to Jesus.

The book belongs to Altemus's Mother Stories series. Companion volumes cover nursery rhymes, fairy tales, nature stories, and the Old Testament. The series title tells its method: simple, warm retellings sized for a mother's lap. Sunday schools and families used such volumes to give children the Gospels' stories before they could read the Bible themselves.
mother-stories-from-the-old-testament-a-:
Henry Altemus of Philadelphia issued this companion storybook in his Mother Stories series. It retells the best stories from the Old Testament for mothers to tell their children. Forty-five illustrations are included. The frontispiece shows Joseph sold into captivity by his brothers.

The series also offered nursery rhymes, fairy tales, nature stories, and a New Testament volume. Each book kept the same promise: the best stories, simply told. Genesis patriarchs, Exodus wonders, and kings and prophets become bedtime narratives here. Such retellings shaped many children's first knowledge of the Bible, long before they met its harder language.
nasa-tm-19660001918-the-response-of-magn:
Folke Eleman, working at Goddard under a research associateship, wrote this June 1965 study on a curious effect. Magnetic instruments on the ground can respond to earthquake waves. The great Alaskan earthquake of 1964 gave a strong case to examine. Two causes are weighed in the catalog note, magnetic changes in rock and electric currents in the ground.

Strained rock can change its magnetism as a wave passes. Currents induced in conductive ground can also disturb a magnetometer. Either effect mixes earthquake signal into magnetic records. Observers need to know that mix to read their data cleanly. Eleman's study treats a problem where Earth science and space science share the same instruments.
nasa-tm-19660009083-system-requirements-: System requirements for a satellite transponder built around a special traveling wave tube are the stated subject of this Goddard report. A transponder receives a signal from the ground and sends it back at a new frequency. The design here passes radio frequency in and radio frequency out directly, using a re-entrant tube as converter. The hosted sample preserves only a subject category list, so no author, date, or detailed requirements can be grounded from it.
nasa-tm-19680006069-evolution-toward-a-s:
John Michael Kemp, of the George Washington University Law School, wrote this historical analysis in September 1966. It traces the evolution toward a space treaty. The paper was his contribution to a NASA seminar on history, social science, and space, run by the NASA Historical Staff.

Kemp began by documenting precedents for a celestial bodies treaty. President Johnson had proposed such a treaty in May 1966. As the research grew, a chronology was not enough. The work became a narrative account with historical analysis instead. It records how the rules for outer space were argued into being.
nasa-tm-19690018477-on-the-nature-of-the:
Reuven Ramaty of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this May 1969 paper on the high-frequency cutoffs of Type IV solar radio bursts. Type IV bursts are broad radio emissions that follow some solar flares. Their spectra rise to a peak, then fall away sharply at high frequencies. Ramaty asks what physical effect trims the top of the spectrum so cleanly.

He investigates synchrotron radiation from electrons whose pitch angles are not spread evenly.
